items.title: Fewer products, more proof: who is winning the healthspan economy?

speakers.name: Nick Stene
speakers.role: Senior Global Insight Manager, Consumer Health

items.to_check: Room not on the agenda. Billed 09:20 to 09:40 on the printed agenda (Nathan's photo, 10 Nov 2026); his recording ran 09:24 to 09:47, as the day ran late.
items.added_by: Claude (from Nathan's Otter recording, 10 Nov 2026)

summary.Summary:
Nick Stene, Senior Global Insight Manager for consumer health at Euromonitor International, opened the Healthspan Summit. His question was where the money in healthspan is going and which messages earn a premium.

He started with the market. Consumer health grows about 5%, only 1.5% without inflation, and this is the first year more is spent on prevention than on treatment. Medicines sold over the counter and sports protein are both under profit pressure, so money, including billions in deal finance, is moving to premium dietary supplements.

Within healthspan, products that name a specific need or life stage earn a premium, while broad wording appears on cheap and expensive products alike. Ingredients follow a life cycle: proof brings a premium, popularity brings scale, then a price war. Magnesium forms have gone that way and NAD+ is close, with postbiotics leading what queues behind it. IM8, one product meant to replace a shelf of supplements, was his example of a brand winning on proof and trust.

His conclusion: lead with proof, know where each ingredient is in its life cycle, segment and price for specific groups such as women entering perimenopause, and design proof for shoppers, healthcare professionals and the AI agents that will increasingly shop for them.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Milestone: "the first year in which we have spent more physically on prevention than we have on treatment", and the gap between supplements and OTC will widen [00:20] (photo 2).
- Money is moving to premium dietary supplements, through line extensions, brand actions and M&A; he sees "about eight to $9 billion in motion", some from venture capital and private equity outside health [00:20].
- Healthspan as a funnel: the edge (SKU names directly on age and life stage, including mitochondrial) is niche, growing and earns a premium; broader healthspan wording appears on cheap and expensive products alike; protection messages (immune, antioxidant) cover about half the shelf [00:20].
- Ingredient life cycle: proof of benefit, then premium, then popularity, then price war. Magnesium forms "turned into footballs" on price, while L-threonate, the cognitive form, still holds a premium; "popularity is the death knell on premium" [00:20] (photo 3).
- NAD+ is losing its premium as it goes mainstream (US price index 1.84 in 2024, 1.43 in 2026 to date); postbiotics lead what queues behind it, with share up 48% and a price index of 2.83 [00:20] (photo 4).
- IM8 is the fastest year-one growth he has seen: one product of 90 ingredients positioned to replace 16 supplements, with year-two revenue guidance of USD 220 to 230 million [00:20] (photo 7).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- He expects premium whey supply to start being solved around the back end of 2027, 2028 at the earliest, and sees sports protein brands passing on 20% or more on shelf, 30 to 40% with smaller packs [00:20]. Alan Johnstone at SANS Europe expects whey to stay structurally expensive, with announced capacity running to 2028 (unfiltered-an-insider-s-view-of). My reading: both views point to protein margins staying tight through 2027, which keeps blends and alternatives such as IsoClr: Pea on brands' agendas.
- His ingredient life cycle applies to creatine: proof brings a premium and popularity erodes it [00:20] (photo 3). My reading: CreaWin's case to brands should rest on its own evidence and a clear benefit, not on creatine's popularity.
- Healthy-ageing customers pay for named needs and proof, and in Europe mitochondrial wording is already established [00:20]. My reading: our healthy-ageing pitches should name the need and the evidence.
- AI shopping agents read proof differently [00:20]. My reading: our evidence files should be structured and machine-readable.
- Relevance high: healthy-ageing market structure and sports protein economics.

- "...we've got to name the need, and the more we name the need, the more we get the benefits out of this space" Speaker 1 (Nick Stene) [00:20]
- "...popularity is the death knell on premium." Speaker 1 (Nick Stene) [00:20]

- Nick Stene (Euromonitor): ask for the deck and the premium-versus-launch data for sports protein and creatine [00:20].
- The next speaker, introduced as "Emma Hudson, senior insights director" in Otter's transcript, was Ewa Hudson of Lumina Intelligence; her talk is filed as lumina-new-longevity-consumer [23:16].

summary.Detail:
- The speaker was introduced as Nick Steen; the title slide gives Nick Stene, Senior Global Insight Manager, Consumer Health, Euromonitor International [00:00] (photo 1).
- Market: he gave consumer health as "373 billion", growing about 5%, or 1.5 without inflation, half a point down; treatment has gone negative in real terms [00:20]. The slide gives USD 373 billion, +5% in current terms (3.5% price rises) and +1.5% without inflation ("demand stagnation") (photo 2).
- Growth by category, 2025 then 2026: vitamins and dietary supplements 5.9% and 5.6%; OTC 3.4% and 3.2%; sports nutrition 13.3% and 12.5%; weight management and wellbeing 0.2% and 0.3%. Shares of the market: vitamins and supplements 42%, OTC 42%, sports nutrition 11%, weight management and wellbeing 5%. The slide's line: "2026 is the year when we started spending more on prevention than we do on treatment" (photo 2).
- OTC is hit hardest by tariffs, by dependence on active pharmaceutical ingredients from India and China, and, next, by European wastewater rules [00:20].
- Sports protein, as he said it: he has shelf data showing a 20% plus pass-through in physical pricing, 30 to 40% overall once pack shrinkage and other absorption moves are counted. On premium whey supply: "So the protein one probably starts to get solved in supply because it's scarcity driven around premium way around 2027 back end, 2028 earliest", with "years of trauma" left [00:20].
- Growth is stronger in shops than online, where trust is leaking; demographics explain about 30 to 40% of growth (people entering a new life stage, not the size of the ageing population), brand push about another third, and employers' attitudes to time off work more [00:20].
- On the US shelf, longevity and healthy ageing grow fastest and earn a strong premium; menopause is losing its premium while 40-plus and perimenopause still earn one; prostate has lost its premium; skin peaked in 2025 and hair is next; immune has peaked but remains a workhorse [00:20].
- Europe follows the same pattern, but mitochondrial messaging is already stronger than in the US, partly because of what the regulatory framework allows, and healthy-ageing messaging is "a tougher sell", some of it only online [00:20].
- Magnesium forms in Europe, January to August 2026 against 2025, read approximately from the chart (price index against matched peers, change in share of products): carbonate about 1.4 and 0%; oxide about 0.75 and 3%; citrate about 0.95 and 13%; bisglycinate about 0.65 and 42%; taurate about 0.55 and 43%; malate about 0.55 and 48%; L-threonate (cognitive) about 1.17 and 49%. The slide's line: "Popularity is a consistent death [k]nell for premium [achieve]ment." (photo 3). Otter heard L-threonate as "L3 and eight" [00:20].
- NAD+ escaped niche last year and grew three times on the US shelf in 18 months; stacks with spermidine and resveratrol won back some premium in 2026, but it is near price war [00:20]. The slide's NAD+ family price index (NAD+, NADH, NR, NMN, NMNH): US 1.84 in 2024, 1.28 in 2025, 1.43 in 2026 to date; Europe 1.68, 1.50 and 1.32 (photo 4).
- Queuing behind NAD+, US 2026 (share growth, price index): postbiotics +48%, 2.83; urolithin A +17%, 1.37; TMG +19%, 1.23; fisetin +22%, 1.14; spermidine +45%, 1.13. The slide's line: "What's next? Because nothing stays shiny and new forev[er]" (photo 4).
- Postbiotics are growing fast, have "really strong connections into GLP-1" and earn one of the strongest premiums; he is watching them most closely. In his words: "But postbiotics is at this moment in time kicking ass" [00:20].
- Life stage, US products per 10,000 supplement products, 2024, 2025 and 2026 to date: testosterone 171, 182, 163; prostate 70, 85, 98; menopause 46, 64, 73; andropause 0, 1, 2. The slides: perimenopause is picking up fast while menopause slows; andropause is "near non-existent on the shelf"; testosterone is more than twice the size of menopause on the shelf, stalled in the US, still rising in Europe and getting cheaper, with fading spikes in tongkat ali, tribulus and shilajit; prostate support now rises fast (photo 5) (photo 6).
- Men do not buy into an andropause label; they respond to testosterone, performance and prostate messages [00:20] (photo 6).
- IM8, as he said it: over 100 million in year one, on target for 220 to 230 in year two, 400 million projected for year three, and a billion raised on a profitable subscription model [00:20]. The slide: year-two revenue guidance USD 220 to 230 million and 2027 full-year guidance over USD 400 million; US online sales peaked in Q4 2025 and eased slightly in Q1 and Q2 2026; the US is by far its largest market, ahead of the UK and Canada (photo 7).
- Why IM8 wins, from the slide: one product replaces a shelf (90 ingredients, positioned to replace 16 other supplements); celebrity equity and a science council, driving word of mouth; subscription economics a lender can fund, with USD 1.44 of declared gross profit per USD 1 of acquisition; and an AI-native acquisition engine across 43 markets. "IM8 nailed "trust" in all its flavours" (photo 7).
- He named IM8 and Ancient + Brave as brands nailing proof [00:20]. Nathan's note: IM8 "is winning a lot in the market, alongside Ancient+Brave" (notes).
- Positioning that facilitates "someone's perfect life" lasts longer than solving a problem, which ends when it is fixed or fails; collagen can be sold either way [00:20]. The slide sets "something wrong [with] you our product can fix" (joints, wrinkles, ageing, collagen deficiency) against "Aspire to a life free of imperfection" (vitality, performance, radiance, wellbeing): "you never stop taking something that is part of who you want to be" (photo 8).
- His takeaways: lead with proof; know the ingredient's life stage and the pipeline behind it; segment and price, with women heading into perimenopause badly served; and design proof for three gatekeepers: shoppers, healthcare professionals and agentic commerce [00:20].

items.title: Too Young to Age? The New Consumer Rules of Longevity
items.to_check: Ewa Hudson's role at Lumina Intelligence and the room are not confirmed. Title and slot (09:40 to 09:55) from the printed agenda (Nathan's photo, 10 Nov 2026); her recording ran 09:47 to 10:05. Otter's "Niagara" is probably Niagen; the 27% bar on photo 1 is not clearly on the Retired series.
items.added_by: Claude (from Nathan's slide photos and Otter recording, 10 Nov 2026)

summary.Summary:
Ewa Hudson of Lumina Intelligence presented consumer research on ageing from a survey of over 10,000 people in nine countries. Her question: consumers are rewriting the rules of ageing, so is the industry ready to rewrite its own?

Her first point was that the longevity consumer is no longer old. Retired people mostly began thinking seriously about ageing in their 60s; people in full-time work mostly in their 30s. Younger people blame their genes less and put more faith in supplements, and one in four is actively pursuing anti-ageing.

Ageing well, she said, means having the vitality to keep reinventing yourself. She named energy, stamina and physical strength as the top concern across age brackets, and mobility, joint and bone health as first for women. Needs shift with life stage and country, and GLP-1 treatment is moving users towards healthier habits.

Trust is the gap: the first answer on hesitation about longevity supplements was not enough proof. Some brands are moving from selling supplements to measuring biological ageing, as Life Extension does with blood tests taken before and after supplements. Her conclusion: applied and communicated science will be the number one trust creator, and the leaders of the next decade may be platforms that measure, manage and optimise ageing.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Concern about ageing starts younger: retired respondents mostly began thinking seriously about it in their 60s (36% on the Retired bar), people in full-time work mostly in their 30s; she called it "a generational shift" [00:04] (photo 1).
- The younger the respondent, the less they credit genetics and the more they credit supplements: genetics from 39% at 65 plus down to 21% in the youngest group; supplements from 20% at 25 to 34 down to 12% at 65 plus [00:04].
- "[1 in] 4 is actively pursuing [anti]-ageing": 16% want to prevent premature ageing and 11% to reverse it, beside 52% who want to age slowly and healthily [00:04] (photo 2).
- Energy, stamina and strength is in the top three concerns of every age band shown, for men and women; mobility, joint and bone health is in the top three of every band from 35 to 44 up for both, and from 25 to 34 for women (photo 3).
- Trust is the gap: the first answer to "What's your biggest hesitation about taking longevity supplements?" was not enough proof; 36% already take supplements to counteract natural ageing [00:04].
- Brands are moving from selling supplements to managing biological ageing: Life Extension sells ageing blood tests to take before and after supplements, and she gave Novos as "Another similar example" of a move "from supplement brand to health intelligence company" [00:04] (photo 4).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Energy, stamina and strength is a top-three ageing concern in every age band for both men and women (photo 3). My reading: this is the concern our sports and active nutrition ingredients (CreaWin, IsoClr: Pea, Oxystorm) sit closest to, so healthy-ageing brands are a natural audience for them, pitched within what each ingredient's own evidence supports. The slide gives an order of concerns, not percentages.
- Working people start thinking about ageing in their 30s [00:04] (photo 1). My reading: the healthy-ageing buyer and the active adult our customers already sell to are increasingly the same person, which widens where sports ingredients can be pitched.
- Proof is the first hesitation, and brands such as Life Extension now test before and after supplements [00:04] (photo 4). My reading: brands will ask suppliers for clinical evidence and outcomes a consumer can measure; our evidence files should be ready for that.
- Science published behind the scenes "will feed all the AI tools" consumers now ask for advice [00:04]. My reading: our evidence should be public and easy for those tools to read.
- Relevance high: consumer data on ageing, with energy and strength as the leading concern.
summary.Quotes:
- "...the younger you are, the less you blame your genes." Speaker 1 (Ewa Hudson) [00:04]
- "Aging well means actually having the vitality to keep reinventing yourself." Speaker 1 (Ewa Hudson) [00:04]
- "...trust is the gap and is costing the industry." Speaker 1 (Ewa Hudson) [00:04]
- "So applied and communicated science will be definitely the number one trust creator" Speaker 1 (Ewa Hudson) [00:04]
summary.Follow-ups:
- Ewa Hudson (Lumina Intelligence): ask for the deck, the full survey (the ninth country, the lighter series on photo 1, the 18% who want to stay as they are) and the UK GLP-1 tracker [00:04].
- Confirm "Niagara" (probably Niagen) and "Novos" with the deck or the speaker.
- The billed title, her role and the track, once the programme is published.
summary.Key slides:
- (photo 1) Age at which retired respondents first thought seriously about ageing: mostly their 60s.
- (photo 2) One in four actively pursuing anti-ageing: 52% age slowly, 16% prevent, 11% reverse.
- (photo 3) Top three ageing concerns by age band, men and women, with energy and mobility traced through the ages.
- (photo 4) Life Extension's ageing lab tests: from supplement brand to health intelligence company.
summary.Detail:
- The whole talk is one Otter turn starting at [00:04], labelled Speaker 1; Stephen Daniells (NutraIngredients) thanks her at [17:12]. Neither the recording nor the slides give her billed title or role.
- Her three parts: longevity aspirations across generations, what consumers want and need, and whether scientific innovation on its own is enough to earn consumers' trust [00:04].
- Survey base, as she said it: over 10,000 people in nine countries [00:04]. Photo 3 names Brazil, China, France, Germany, Italy, Saudi Arabia, Spain and the UK along its foot; the ninth is cut off (photo 3).
- What most extends healthspan: respondents agreed on exercise, sleep and diet. Genetics as a big factor: 39% at 65 plus, 50% in Italy and Saudi Arabia, then 31, 26, 24, 23 and 21% in each younger group [00:04].
- Supplements as having a role: 20 at 25 to 34, then 19%, 17% and 12% at 65 plus; she linked the 12% to retired people starting to think about ageing in their 60s [00:04].
- Photo 1, "[The] new longevity consumer isn't old yet: [age]ing has shifted from a retirement concern to [a] 30-something priority": the Retired bars read 1% (20s), 3% (30s), 10% (40s), 36% (60s) and 11% (70s); 27% is printed at the 50s, but the photo does not show whether it belongs to the Retired bar or the lighter one; 10% have not started yet (photo 1). The lighter bars have no visible label and no printed values; they are tallest for the 20s, 30s and 40s (photo 1). In the talk she compared retired people with "the working population and full-time employment", most of whom were in their 30s [00:04]. My reading: the lighter bars are probably that working group, but the photo does not say so.
- Ageing goals: 52% want to age slowly and healthily, 16% to prevent premature ageing, 11% to reverse ageing (photo 2). She added "another 18% want to stay just as they are", which the photo does not show [00:04].
- Ambition with age, as Otter heard it: a US Census study of 2.7 million founders found the fastest-growing 0.1% of new ventures were founded at 45 on average, and a 50-year-old was "roughly 1.1 times as likely" as a 30-year-old to found an exceptional-growth company; British Business Bank data for 2024 show a boom in over-50 entrepreneurs in the UK; runners who start in their 70s to 90s run marathons at 100 [00:04].
- Photo 3, "[Agei]ng well means having the vitality to keep [rein]venting yourself", "biggest health-related concerns as we age? Top 3", concerns listed left to right (the slide does not say the order is a rank) (photo 3):
  - Men list energy, stamina and strength first from 18 to 24 through 55 to 64; at 65 plus mobility, joint and bone health comes first, then energy, then cognitive decline.
  - Women list emotional wellbeing first at 18 to 24 and weight first at 25 to 34; mobility, joint and bone health comes first in every band from 35 to 44 up. Cognitive decline appears at 55 to 64 and loss of independence at 65 plus.
  - Weight appears in two men's and three women's bands; chronic diseases in three men's bands and one women's.
- In her words, products need to give consumers "energy and physical strength, mobility, joint health, weight management, cognitive, and everyday activity support and recovery" [00:04].
- Companies reinventing themselves: Otter heard "Niagara" (probably Niagen; to check), "from product to purpose", with "500 studies" and "100 patents" as heard, moving into services (IV injections, cosmetics) and into pharma [00:04].
- Life stages, women: at 35 to 44 sleep is "much more important at any other age"; she said messages on cellular energy renewal, and on cellular defence declining from about 30, will resonate. Ten years later sleep matters less and weight management, exercise, gut health and muscle strength come up; in Italy preventative medical testing matters more. She said "The previous data was for the UK and Italy" [00:04].
- Life stages, men: in their 30s sleep, stress and exercise; ten years later healthy eating over-indexes and they are much more into supplements [00:04].
- GLP-1 users, top three changes: more interest in healthy foods, longevity and preventative health; less alcohol, eating and drinking out of home, and snacking. Lumina runs a GLP-1 trends tracker focused on the UK [00:04].
- 36%, "one in three", already take supplements to counteract natural ageing: vitamins, omegas, minerals, probiotics, postbiotics and more, varying by sex and life stage [00:04].
- Life Extension's ageing tests on photo 4: Phenotypic Age Project Panel blood test USD 105.00 ("Test key aging markers and calculate biological age"); Healthy Aging Panel (Comprehensive) USD 249.00; Healthy Aging Panel (Basic) USD 155.00; MTHFR/COMT genetic methylation cheek swab USD 149.00. The slide asks "How do we help people understand their biology? Supplement brand -> Health intelligence company" (photo 4). She gave the biological-age blood test as "for $100" [00:04].
- Her reading of test and retest: it shows a brand's trust in its ingredients, a positive result may make the most loyal consumers, and it is "a way of going around the health legislation a little bit" because "whatever is on the back is becoming less relevant" [00:04].
- On the slide the "health intelligence company" line sits under the Life Extension screenshot (photo 4); in the talk she applied the words to Novos, as heard, as "Another similar example" [00:04].
- "the health plan leaders of the next decade may not be the pure product companies themselves", but platforms "that measure, manage, and optimize aging" [00:04].
- At the NutraIngredients Awards the healthy-ageing category (Otter: "health fund") is among the most popular, with the most submissions [00:04].
- She closed with consumers' hopes for wellness technology in 2040 and a quote from Jonas Salk [00:04].

takeaways.text: Concern about ageing starts younger: retired respondents mostly began thinking seriously about it in their 60s (36% on the Retired bar), people in full-time work mostly in their 30s; she called it "a generational shift" [00:04] (photo 1).

"[1 in] 4 is actively pursuing [anti]-ageing": 16% want to prevent premature ageing and 11% to reverse it, beside 52% who want to age slowly and healthily [00:04] (photo 2).

Energy, stamina and strength is in the top three concerns of every age band shown, for men and women; mobility, joint and bone health is in the top three of every band from 35 to 44 up for both, and from 25 to 34 for women (photo 3).
Trust is the gap: the first answer to "What's your biggest hesitation about taking longevity supplements?" was not enough proof; 36% already take supplements to counteract natural ageing [00:04].

Brands are moving from selling supplements to managing biological ageing: Life Extension sells ageing blood tests to take before and after supplements, and she gave Novos as "Another similar example" of a move "from supplement brand to health intelligence company" [00:04] (photo 4).

summary.Summary:
Stephen Daniells of NutraIngredients chaired two retailers, a brand and a marketplace: Jessica Pasco of Holland & Barrett, Rachel Kreider of GNC, Federico Luna of Timeline and Jennifer Wang of Alibaba's Taobao Tmall. His question: is longevity a real category, or an umbrella for outcomes consumers already understand?

They agreed that shoppers pay for benefits they can feel or see. Prevention alone is hard to sell, so proof and a tangible result, such as stronger muscles or better skin, matter most. They also agreed that GLP-1 medicines move people into a proactive mindset, and that creatine and muscle are a way into healthy ageing.

They differed on the category itself. Luna said longevity is absolutely a category, defined by the hallmarks of ageing and four pillars, and that bundling a generic vitamin C into it does consumers a disservice. Pasco said Holland & Barrett's new in-store longevity category is small but growing fast, driven mainly by NAD, while most proactive shopping is not badged longevity. Kreider said GNC treats healthy ageing as a demand space and links new ingredients to condition-specific products. Wang said nobody in China searches for longevity online: men search for sexual vitality and women for sagging skin, and premium shoppers ask for patents and clinical studies.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Holland & Barrett created a longevity category in store over the last six months; it is "still quite small" but has seen "really significant growth", driven primarily by NAD, with spermidine less popular [02:58] [03:47].
- GNC defines healthy ageing as a target demand space and is extending its condition-specific preventive nutrition brand into standalone longevity ingredients such as NAD+; Kreider said consumers need to connect it to a benefit they can feel [08:44].
- Online in China, longevity is not a search term: the trigger for men is sexual vitality and for women sagging skin, followed by joints, sleep and metabolism [06:09].
- GLP-1 as a gateway: Pasco sees customers entering the category because they start a GLP-1 journey and staying after they stop the medication [14:52]; Kreider sees an opportunity for products that protect muscle on that journey [15:59].
- Creatine is crossing over: Kreider said people engage with healthy ageing through creatine and active nutrition, and Pasco said creatine is "moving from a more of a sports focus into this longevity space" [17:19] [19:15].
- Proof decides the role of an ingredient: Kreider wants hero ingredients with clinical substantiation and a tangible benefit, with buzzier ingredients as background [31:12]; Wang said Chinese shoppers ask for a branded ingredient, a patent and a clinical study, and pay the premium [22:45].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Two major retailers, GNC and Holland & Barrett, both see creatine moving from sports into healthy ageing [17:19] [19:15]. My reading: CreaWin can be pitched to healthy-ageing ranges, on its own evidence for muscle.
- GLP-1 users are entering the supplement aisle and staying, and muscle protection is the named need [14:52] [15:59]. My reading: protein and creatine for muscle on a GLP-1 journey are a pitch retailers already recognise.
- Retailers want hero ingredients with clinical substantiation and a benefit the shopper can feel [08:44] [31:12]. My reading: our pitches to healthy-ageing brands should lead with a felt outcome and the study behind it, not a mechanism.
- Chinese premium shoppers ask for branded ingredients, patents and studies, and Chinese brands combine several branded ingredients in one product [22:45]. My reading: Tmall cross-border is a channel where branded, documented ingredients earn their price.
- Relevance high: retailer category structure for healthy ageing, creatine and GLP-1 muscle.

- "...I do think that consumers need to be able to connect it to a benefit" Rachel @ GNC (Rachel Kreider) [08:44]

summary.Summary:
Professor Jens Walter of University College Cork and APC Microbiome Ireland, a co-founder of Synbiotic Health, asked whether the gut microbiome shapes how we age, and whether diet or supplements that target it could extend healthspan.

He started with animal studies. Germ-free rodents live longer than normal ones, but with calorie restriction the microbiome becomes beneficial, so its effect depends on diet. In humans, large observational studies link healthy eating patterns to healthy ageing; one UK study suggests a healthy diet can add about ten years of healthier life if adopted in your 40s and 50s.

His own trial in Cell put students on a high-fibre, non-industrialised diet for three weeks. Bifidobacteria rose, inflammatory bacteria fell, and LDL cholesterol dropped by 17%. Older people rarely change their whole diet, so he sees room for alternatives: Bifidobacterium adolescentis, which falls with age and is linked with healthy ageing, paired with fibre.

He kept his hedges. Causality is clearly established in animals only, there is no direct evidence yet that the microbiome mediates diet's effects in humans, and clinical trials are needed. His company's trials in older people have not reported. In questions he doubted that postbiotics can change gut ecology.
summary.Key takeaways:
- In animal studies, rodents kept without a microbiome live almost ten months longer than normal mice, which live about 25 months; with calorie restriction the microbiome becomes beneficial and those animals live longest [00:24].
- Observational studies in humans link healthy dietary patterns to healthy ageing; one UK study found a healthy diet can extend healthier lifespan by ten years, adopted in the 40s and 50s, and "probably" five to six years if adopted in the 70s [00:24].
- His Cell trial of a non-industrialised, higher-fibre diet in students over three weeks raised bifidobacteria and indole-3-propionic acid, lowered faecal pH and secondary bile acids, cut LDL cholesterol by 17% and reduced blood glucose and CRP [00:24].
- Bifidobacterium adolescentis falls with age and is associated with healthy ageing (centenarians in Sardinia, slower epigenetic ageing in about 123 people); in animal studies it improved healthspan and lifespan; human trials in older people by Synbiotic Health are ongoing, with no data yet [00:24].
- His conclusion: the microbiome is a plausible contributor to healthy ageing, established in animal models; causality is hard to establish in humans and clinical trials are needed [00:24].
- He is doubtful that a postbiotic can change gut ecology or raise short-chain fatty acids, prefers probiotic bifidobacteria with fibre, and sees a possible role for postbiotics in a direct immune effect [22:01] [22:52].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- He sees the next healthy-ageing supplements as probiotic bifidobacteria combined with fibre, because older people rarely change their whole diet [00:24]. My reading: fibre for healthy ageing may be pitched as a partner to probiotics, within what the evidence supports, which he says is not yet proven in humans.
- He cited animal research in which high-protein diets shorten lifespan, and said he is not sure how far it translates to humans [00:24]. My reading: brands selling protein for healthy ageing may hear this; our answer should rest on human muscle evidence.
- Postbiotics divide the speakers: Nick Stene of Euromonitor sees them leading the ingredients queuing behind NAD+, with share up 48% and one of the strongest price premiums (euromonitor-who-is-winning-healthspan), while Walter doubts they can change gut ecology [22:01]. Both views are given.
- Relevance medium: healthy-ageing science around fibre and probiotics; protein comes up only through animal studies.
summary.Quotes:
- "...the microbiome is a plausible contributor to healthy aging in animal model." Speaker 1 (Jens Walter) [00:24]
- "...we don't really have any direct evidence that the microbiome is mediating these these diet effects." Speaker 1 (Jens Walter) [00:24]
- "...by eating a healthy diet, you can extend your healthier lifespan by 10 years." Speaker 1 (Jens Walter) [00:24]
- "...I'm not sure a postbiotic can achieve that." Speaker 1 (Jens Walter) [22:52]
summary.Follow-ups:
- Jens Walter: the Synbiotic Health trials in older people, when they report, and its B. adolescentis and fibre combination [00:24].
- Find his Cell paper on the non-industrialised diet and the UK study on ten years of healthier life [00:24].
- Confirm his affiliation as introduced (University College Cork, APC Microbiome Ireland).

- Paul O'Toole's work (a Nature paper of 2013): with age, pathogens rise and healthy bacteria fall, with links to inflammation and lower barrier function; the microbiome declines further when older people move into nursing homes, probably linked to diet [00:24].
- Bifidobacteria make a dramatic dive with ageing; observational research cannot establish cause and effect [00:24].
- Animal studies: the germ-free lifespan finding has been repeated in mice, rats and other species; "in a lot of animal models, high protein diets actually shorten lifespan. Not sure to what degree this then translates to human." [00:24]
- A Nature Medicine paper of large cohorts: healthy dietary patterns link to healthy ageing; an unhealthy vegetarian pattern does the least good; the alternative healthy eating index (vegetables, fruit, whole grains, nuts, legumes, omega-3, little industrialised and high-sugar food) has the most convincing link; small amounts of wine are linked to healthier ageing [00:24].
- A systematic review published a week or two before the talk links Mediterranean diet adherence, partly from intervention studies, to healthy ageing outcomes [00:24].
- O'Toole's Mediterranean diet study in 612 older people: lower levels of bacteria associated with frailty and cognition, links to lower inflammatory ageing, higher short-chain fatty acids and fewer secondary bile acids, which he said drive colon cancer [00:24].
- His Cell trial, two years ago: a non-industrialised diet close to Mediterranean, slightly higher in fibre and lower in saturated fat, in students, not older people; bifidobacteria including B. adolescentis and B. longum rose; inflammatory bacteria fell; proteolytic fermentation fell; indole-3-propionic acid, a neuroprotective antioxidant with consistent benefits "specifically in mice", rose; participants lost weight [00:24]. The diet gives 45 grams of fibre a day, and the pH drop is "clearly fiber fermentation" [23:38].
- B. adolescentis: enriched in healthy people (Synbiotic Health's data), dominant in adults and reduced in ageing; a keystone species that amplifies fibre's effects; the oldest living person at the time, aged 116, had almost 50% bifidobacteria ("an N of one"); it produces GABA, improved intestinal barrier function in his group's paper, and in a Nature Aging paper regulated catalase activity and improved healthspan and lifespan "in multiple animal species" [00:24].
- Lumina's earlier talk came up: he recalled that "40% of men now in the 40s think healthy eating is actually important" [00:24]. Ewa Hudson's talk as recorded says healthy eating "really over-indexes" for men ten years after their 30s, without a percentage (lumina-new-longevity-consumer). Both are given.
- Human milk oligosaccharides: studies show they can raise bifidobacteria in older people, but "the jury is completely out" on stimulating infant-associated species and on clinical benefit [21:22].
- Short-chain fatty acids are "very very hard to increase", even with extreme diet shifts [22:52].
- Causality: he has been on three or four papers on it; transplant models and C. elegans have limits; causal inference in humans "comes with its own bag of limitations" [23:38].
- The recipes of the non-industrialised diet are free to download [00:24].

takeaways.text: In animal studies, rodents kept without a microbiome live almost ten months longer than normal mice, which live about 25 months; with calorie restriction the microbiome becomes beneficial and those animals live longest [00:24].

Observational studies in humans link healthy dietary patterns to healthy ageing; one UK study found a healthy diet can extend healthier lifespan by ten years, adopted in the 40s and 50s, and "probably" five to six years if adopted in the 70s [00:24].

His Cell trial of a non-industrialised, higher-fibre diet in students over three weeks raised bifidobacteria and indole-3-propionic acid, lowered faecal pH and secondary bile acids, cut LDL cholesterol by 17% and reduced blood glucose and CRP [00:24].

Bifidobacterium adolescentis falls with age and is associated with healthy ageing (centenarians in Sardinia, slower epigenetic ageing in about 123 people); in animal studies it improved healthspan and lifespan; human trials in older people by Synbiotic Health are ongoing, with no data yet [00:24].
His conclusion: the microbiome is a plausible contributor to healthy ageing, established in animal models; causality is hard to establish in humans and clinical trials are needed [00:24].

He is doubtful that a postbiotic can change gut ecology or raise short-chain fatty acids, prefers probiotic bifidobacteria with fibre, and sees a possible role for postbiotics in a direct immune effect [22:01] [22:52].

summary.Summary:
Stephen Daniells of NutraIngredients chaired eight members of the public, who gave their first names and ages: Robert (38), Matt (27), Mike (51), Michelle (64), Rahav (25), Donella (51), Nadine (46) and Kane. He asked what they focus on, where they get their information and how they would take a supplement pitch. The audience asked about the long term, AI and trust.

They agreed on most things. All try to exercise and eat well; supplement use runs from none to four. Natural ingredients win attention; pills and synthetic ingredients put several of them off. They want proof before they buy: the science, an effective dose and independent research. Holland & Barrett earns trust by being long established, and most distrust influencers. Nobody raised price.

They differed in their concerns and their sources. The men named heart, colon and mental health; the women named sleep, menopause, hormones and bones. Michelle follows Ayurveda, Donella wants natural and regenerative sourcing, and Kane takes creatine and protein powder for training. Rahav, the youngest, does not mind non-natural products if a brand explains why she needs them today, and wants trials to say whom they did not test. On AI, Mike checks supplements with ChatGPT and Claude and asks for the evidence; Matt scrolls past AI health answers.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Naturalness opens the conversation: Robert listens more the more natural the product and shuts off at pills [23:46], Matt and Mike said much the same [24:01] [24:34], and Robert named naturalness as the main thing to build into a new product [45:44]. Rahav was the exception: she does not mind non-natural products if she is told how they help her [47:02].
- Proof decides: Michelle wants the science and a dose high enough to be effective [25:28] [25:59], Nadine wants to know whether the research was independent or paid for by a company with a vested interest [31:00], Mike wants clinical trials on the brand's site [42:40], and Rahav wants trials to say honestly whom they were not tested on [43:43].
- Trust comes from time and brand: Mike and Kane trust Holland & Barrett because it has been around a long time [24:34] [31:45]; a new brand, Mike said, needs a mix of advertising, proof on its site and a brand story, and cannot be built overnight [42:40] [47:44].
- Influencers are distrusted: Matt avoids health advice from social media [18:23], Mike asks "what's in it for them" [42:40], and Kane said what works for an influencer may not work for him [31:45]. Their sources are friends, Ayurvedic doctors, an Instagram feed and a Netflix documentary on Blue Zones [10:12] [17:45] [16:37] [20:32].
- AI is used with checks: Mike asks ChatGPT and Claude for evidence and checks it on Google [36:58], Rahav uses AI for low-stakes questions only [38:15], Nadine said AI has to be verified [38:53], and Matt ignores AI on health [37:33].
- Collagen needs a reason today: Rahav wants a collagen pitch to explain why she needs it when her great-grandmother did not [26:18], and Donella wants to know what to take with collagen and where it comes from [28:18].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance high: these are supplement purchase drivers from consumers themselves, with collagen, protein powder and creatine named [05:22] [26:18].
- Origin, naturalness and sustainability came up without prompting [23:46] [28:18] [29:29]. My reading: our ingredients' source, processing and sustainability story should be ready for brand customers' consumer copy, stated only as far as the facts go.
- Dose and independent proof were asked for directly [25:59] [31:00]. My reading: clinically documented ingredients at a stated effective dose give our customers the answer these shoppers asked for.
- Donella asked where collagen comes from, fish or bovine, and what the animals eat [28:18]. My reading: a clear origin and traceability sheet for our collagen would help brands answer that question.
- These are eight people speaking about their own habits: personal experience, not evidence or a market sample (my reading).

summary.Summary:
The recording holds only the last four and a half minutes of Amanda Rao's talk on pharmacokinetic testing, then one audience question. Her argument, in the part recorded: absorption studies are run on the wrong people, in the wrong conditions.

A typical pharmacokinetic study is done on a 25-year-old, while longevity products are typically sold to older women on several medications. GLP-1 medicines slow food through the gut, and studies with paracetamol show lower absorption in people taking them, so they belong in absorption studies. Studies should look at responders and at high and low absorbers, and test products as people take them: with food and coffee, with missed doses and other medications, not fasted and as a single dose.

She sees research moving from single ingredients to whole formulas, and home blood tests making it easy to track blood levels in long-term trials. AI models that predict exposure need good studies to learn from.

Asked about dose, she said a five-dose pharmacokinetic study early on is easier and cheaper than five doses in a long-term trial, and that the industry may need lower doses taken for longer.
summary.Key takeaways:
- In the studies she cited, people on GLP-1 medicines absorbed paracetamol 15 to 50 percent less; absorption studies that leave them out are "not you know, collecting the right data" [00:00].
- Study populations do not match buyers: a typical pharmacokinetic study is on a 25-year-old, while longevity products are typically sold to 65-year-old women on three medications, with low oestrogen and a history of antibiotics [00:00].
- Look at responders and at high and low absorbers, not only at a rise in the blood: "did 90% of people get that?" [00:00].
- Test products as they are taken: most pharmacokinetic studies are fasted and single-dose, while real users eat, drink coffee, miss doses and stack medications [00:00].
- Long-term trials should measure blood levels as well as outcomes, now that home tests are easy; some nutrients, such as iron and vitamin D, need longer studies [00:00].
- On dose, a five-dose pharmacokinetic study early is "easier and honestly cheaper" than five doses in a long-term study; she suggested lower doses for longer [05:14].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance high: this is how absorption evidence for ingredients will be designed and judged, and GLP-1 users are named as a population that absorbs differently [00:00].
- My reading: bioavailability claims for enhanced-absorption forms may be challenged where the study used young, fasted adults; the populations in our studies are worth checking before a pitch to a healthy-ageing brand [00:00].
- My reading: products pitched for muscle on a GLP-1 journey (protein, CreaWin) may in time need absorption data in GLP-1 users before brands rely on them [00:00].
- My reading: a multi-dose pharmacokinetic study is a cheap way to set the dose of a new ingredient before an efficacy trial [05:14].
summary.Quotes:
- "So two people, one capsule, different blood levels." Speaker 1 (Amanda Rao) [00:00]
- "Your typical PK studies done on a 25-year-old." Speaker 1 (Amanda Rao) [00:00]
- "And as we know, real life is messier than the clinic." Speaker 1 (Amanda Rao) [00:00]
- "But maybe we need 10 times less for a longer period of time." Speaker 1 (Amanda Rao) [05:14]

- Find Amanda Rao's organisation, role and slides (the event offers shared presentations through its post-event survey).
- Find the studies on paracetamol absorption in people taking GLP-1 medicines that she cited.
- Check the study populations behind our absorption claims against her points: age, sex, medication, fed or fasted.
summary.Detail:
- Billed 16:15 to 16:35; the recording starts at 16:33, mid-sentence ("Ones that we all we all know and love"), and she closes with "And I think I'm out of time" [00:00]. The start of the talk, her organisation and her slides are not in the folder. Otter merges her talk into one turn, so every point from it cites [00:00].
- Factors she named that change blood levels from one capsule: kidney, liver and hormone changes, medication, genetics, gut microbiome, body composition and BMI, and baseline nutrient status [00:00].
- Sample size: she asked whether a study's sample represents the population the product is for, and answered "probably not" [00:00].
- Finished products: the industry has seen many single-ingredient studies and is moving to how ingredients work together in a whole formula [00:00].
- Home testing: a finger-prick test from a supermarket can show iron deficiency, so long-term studies should add blood concentrations as they go [00:00].
- Methods named: models that predict exposure, stable isotope tracers (Otter: "traces"), and steady-state studies as well as single-point studies [00:00].
- Otter's "using Australian gems" in the GLP-1 passage is unclear [00:00].
- The question came from an audience member (Speaker 4): the dose is often set from 90-day toxicology work, not efficacy; can dose response go into pharmacokinetic studies [04:58]? She said yes; with absorption enhancers the aim is that people feel better, or at least that it gets in without long-term side effects; "it's great to have six times or 10 times more", but lower doses may be needed [05:14].
- The chair (Speaker 3) then moved to wearables, AI and healthspan [06:12], filed as ai-driven-personalization-at-scale.

takeaways.text: In the studies she cited, people on GLP-1 medicines absorbed paracetamol 15 to 50 percent less; absorption studies that leave them out are "not you know, collecting the right data" [00:00].

Study populations do not match buyers: a typical pharmacokinetic study is on a 25-year-old, while longevity products are typically sold to 65-year-old women on three medications, with low oestrogen and a history of antibiotics [00:00].
Look at responders and at high and low absorbers, not only at a rise in the blood: "did 90% of people get that?" [00:00].
Test products as they are taken: most pharmacokinetic studies are fasted and single-dose, while real users eat, drink coffee, miss doses and stack medications [00:00].
Long-term trials should measure blood levels as well as outcomes, now that home tests are easy; some nutrients, such as iron and vitamin D, need longer studies [00:00].
On dose, a five-dose pharmacokinetic study early is "easier and honestly cheaper" than five doses in a long-term study; she suggested lower doses for longer [05:14].

"But maybe we need 10 times less for a longer period of time." Speaker 1 (Amanda Rao) [05:14]

summary.Summary:
Ohad Manor, Vice President of Computational Precision Health at Thorne, argued that supplement shoppers suffer from too much information, not too little. His example was Lena, 47, sleeping badly and wondering about perimenopause, faced with AI answers, social media and influencers.

Personalisation is the answer, he said, but also a double-edged sword: people differ, and so do ingredients, claims and formulations. Thorne has over 250 products, so even its own shoppers struggle to choose. He sees AI as the engine that can personalise at scale, provided it is data-driven, dynamic and educational rather than a black box.

Thorne's answer is Taya, an AI adviser launched in July last year. It works only from Thorne's own products, claims, science and articles, without web access. It asks follow-up questions, narrows its recommendations, adds lifestyle advice and shares articles. By Thorne's count it held over 300,000 conversations in its first year. Manor said it ignores bestsellers and promotions.

He closed by urging supplement companies to build similar tools. Otherwise people go to ChatGPT, which does not know a company's products as its own medical and ingredient teams do.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Thorne's own survey, as Manor gave it: roughly 40% of consumers use AI for health questions, and two out of three would use an AI tool they trusted to make decisions [00:23].
- Taya is a closed system: built on foundation models, but without internet access and limited to Thorne's products, ingredients, claims and science and over 1,000 articles [00:23].
- Thorne's first-year figures for Taya, as Manor gave them: over 300,000 conversations, over 650,000 messages, over 1.2 million product and lifestyle recommendations, over 135,000 articles shared, and about 92% thumbs up [00:23].
- In his Lena example, Taya narrowed eight recommendations to two products, explained the ingredients and gave a daily routine with lifestyle tips [00:23].
- Taya recommends almost the whole portfolio, not the same five products; its top topics in year one were heart health and sports nutrition, then cognition and focus, bone and joint, and metabolism [00:23].
- His call to brands: build such tools, because ChatGPT "doesn't know everything about your products the way you know them" [00:23].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- An AI adviser on a brand's site answers only from that brand's claims and science [00:23]. My reading: the evidence and approved wording we give customers for our ingredients may end up in the knowledge base such a tool reads, so it should be clear and claim-safe.
- Shoppers find ingredient forms confusing; Manor named citrate, glycinate, bisglycinate and threonate forms of magnesium [00:23]. My reading: form-specific evidence is what lets a tool like this choose one product over another.
- Relevance medium: consumer-facing AI at a brand; it touches our ingredients only through the claims and evidence brands feed it.

summary.Summary:
Paul Spagnuolo, a food science professor at the University of Guelph and co-founder and Chief Scientific Officer of Applied Laboratory Technologies (ALT), declared his conflict of interest and explained why he built an AI tool for ingredient discovery.

For 20 years his lab has applied pharmaceutical drug discovery to food molecules, taking two products, one from avocado, from discovery to clinical trial and market. That path is long, costly and mostly fails, and the claim at the end covers only the indication studied.

AMBROSIA, an agentic AI platform built with a computational biologist, aims to shorten the discovery and validation stages. As a retroactive test they gave it the avocado molecule. He said it reached in one day the target and use his lab had taken 10 years and millions of dollars to find. ALT's slide claims the stages shrink from years to days and from millions to thousands.

He said researchers still have to validate in the lab. Finzelberg was the first partner: in less than a week AMBROSIA pointed to how its extract works, which matched Finzelberg's own research. ALT now works business to business, helping companies understand their ingredients and find new markets for them.
summary.Key takeaways:
- ALT's slide claims AMBROSIA cuts discovery and validation from "5-10 years" and millions of dollars to "5-10 days" and thousands (photo 1); Spagnuolo said it took AMBROSIA one day to reach what took his lab 10 years [20:14].
- In ALT's retroactive test on avocatin B, AMBROSIA analysed 1,284 crystal structures and found 361 potential gene targets, 99 at high confidence, with lipid metabolism and PPAR signalling among the primary pathways (photo 2); Spagnuolo said it pointed to acyl-CoA dehydrogenase and fatty acid oxidation [20:14].
- A claim covers only what was studied: a phase two result on cardiometabolic function "that's our claim", not inflammation or longevity [20:14]. ALT pitches AMBROSIA as a way to find new markets for existing ingredients (photo 3) [30:28].
- AI does not replace the lab: "you still need to flip the switch", with researchers doing the validation [20:14].
- Finzelberg, the first partner, received an answer on its extract in less than a week that matched its own research [30:28]; ALT's slide quotes Finzelberg on Menofelis, its Siberian rhubarb extract for menopause, and AMBROSIA's "multi-target profiles" (photo 4).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance high: AI tools that propose mechanisms and new uses change how ingredient evidence is generated, and how fast a supplier can reposition a botanical (photo 3) [30:28].
- A botanical extract supplier, Finzelberg, already uses AMBROSIA to find which compounds in its extract are active and what to study next [30:28]. My reading: a competitor can now get a mechanism map and a study plan for a botanical in days; we should know whether such maps exist for ingredients in our range.
- Spagnuolo was clear that a prediction is not evidence: lab validation and trials are still needed, and a claim covers only the indication studied [20:14]. My reading: an AI target profile could guide a study plan for one of our ingredients, but it supports no claim on its own.

- "Identify new markets for existing ingredients" ALT's slide (photo 3)

Otter heard the platform as "asia", "Embroidery" and "Ambrosia" [20:14]; the slides spell AMBROSIA, "Agentic Multi Modal Biology & Research Operations System for Intelligent Analysis" (photo 1).

- He publishes in high-impact journals because a paper elsewhere could be published "tomorrow" for a few thousand dollars [20:14].
- Formulation work includes a human simulated gastrointestinal system and pharmacokinetic studies [20:14].
- AMBROSIA took about six months to build, with a computational biologist [20:14].

- Finzelberg's text on the slide says AMBROSIA "accelerates the development of effective botanical solutions" and, for Menofelis, identified multi-target profiles across hormone signalling, inflammation and detoxification (photo 4).
- ALT was spun out less than a year ago, after Finzelberg asked at a conference in Europe in November last year what it would cost to use; it now works with "a couple other companies" [30:28]. He called it B2B rather than B2C [30:28].
- He ran 16 seconds over [30:28].

summary.Summary:
Lauren Nicolle of NutraIngredients+ chaired the last session of the day, framed as AI across the product cycle: discovery with Paul Spagnuolo of ALT, clinical validation with Jeff Chen of Radicle Science, and the consumer with Ohad Manor of Thorne.

Chen described Radicle's decentralised, in-house trials, run at home at a scale site studies cannot reach. On hallucinations, Spagnuolo said they happen all the time and ALT keeps its tool inside the scientific literature. Manor said Taya is a closed system and every message is monitored. Chen said narrow knowledge bases and checking agents cut the risk.

Chen argued that home tests, wearables and phones now let trials collect data sites never could, and that machine learning is needed to read it. He wants biomarkers, wearables and surveys combined rather than one trusted alone. Manor said Taya has limits: complicated cases need a healthcare provider, and shoppers should ask who built a tool and on what data.

All three saw true personalisation as some way off. Spagnuolo pointed to genetics and lifestyle, Chen to precision groups first and trial and error over time, Manor to levels of personalisation. Asked about small studies, Chen called for scale and real-world diversity. Stephen Daniells then closed the day.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Chen said Radicle Science has put about 100,000 people through double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trials in about six years, and is running a US-government-funded mental health trial of 6,000 people with one shared placebo and 19 treatment arms [34:11].
- Guardrails against hallucination: ALT keeps AMBROSIA from going outside the literature [36:40]; Thorne monitors and scores every Taya message and sends flagged ones to regulatory and medical [37:43]; Chen said narrow knowledge bases and checking agents cut the risk [39:03].
- Chen: home kits, wearables and phones let decentralised trials collect data sites cannot; agents can automate the "multi-100-step process" of a trial, and machine learning is needed to read the data [39:58]. Biomarkers, wearables and surveys each show one part, so he wants them combined [43:09].
- Small studies: an audience member said many industry studies are pilots of 45-50 or 100 people [58:46]; Spagnuolo said nutraceutical trials run to tens or hundreds, against tens of thousands in pharma [59:13]; Chen said the FDA and NIH are shifting funding toward decentralised approaches [59:31].
- Spagnuolo called for publishing what did not work, since "There's no journal of unpublishable results" [53:38].
- Chen sees a new chance for brands to show consumers, with their own data, that a product delivers its promise [1:02:46].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance high: how ingredient evidence will be generated and judged. Large decentralised trials, run at home, can test many products head to head in parallel [34:11] [59:31]. My reading: a brand could test our ingredient against competitors' in one trial; Radicle is worth a call on cost and design.
- Pilot studies of a few dozen people were challenged from the floor and by the panel [58:46] [59:13]. My reading: the small studies behind many ingredient claims may carry less weight as larger, real-world trials become common.
- Chen's point that consumers can see a product work in their own wearable data [1:02:46]. My reading: felt outcomes such as sleep or strength, measured at home, could become part of how brands using our ingredients sell them.
- Spagnuolo's call for negative results [53:38]. My reading: worth knowing which of our ingredients' unpublished studies a brand or regulator might ask about.
summary.Quotes:
- "...so hallucinations all the time." Speaker 4 (Paul Spagnuolo) [36:40]
- "We put about 100,000 people through double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials." Speaker 7 (Jeff Chen) [34:11]
- "There's no journal of unpublishable results, right?" Speaker 4 (Paul Spagnuolo) [53:38]
- "...you can construct a beautiful trial that's just not real world" Speaker 7 (Jeff Chen) [59:31]
summary.Follow-ups:
- Jeff Chen (Radicle Science): cost and design of a decentralised trial for one of our ingredients, including head-to-head arms.
- Fill in the post-event survey to get the presentations [1:05:01].
- Find out who the "creatine OG" on the next day's programme is [1:05:01]; relevant to CreaWin.

- Billed 17:10 to 17:45, with the Chair's Closing Remarks at 17:45; recorded 17:13 to 17:46. Speaker labels: Speaker 1 is Lauren Nicolle, Speaker 2 Ohad Manor, Speaker 4 Paul Spagnuolo, Speaker 7 Jeff Chen; Speaker 3 at [58:46], Speaker 8 and Speaker 9 are audience members; Speakers 5 and 6 are fragments. Otter heard "Dr. Ernie Manna", "porn", "Jack Chen" and "Radical Science" [33:02]; the speaker slide gives Ohad Manor, Thorne, Jeff Chen and Radicle Science (photo 1).
- Jeff Chen gave no separate talk in the recording; he introduced Radicle inside the panel [34:11]. Its platform runs what it calls reflexive trials, which get smarter the more trials it runs; it holds several patents and does recruitment, biostatistics, medical writing and safety monitoring in house [34:11].
- The 6,000-person study measures, as Otter heard them, "cardiomyopaths, metabolomics, dual microbiome, continuous glucose monitoring, all in home" [34:11].
- Spagnuolo: AI could replace graduate students in making some decisions quickly; its limit is that validation in the lab, and even a clinical trial, are still needed [35:55]. Building the guardrails took the most time [36:40].
- Manor: Taya could have been built in a day by connecting it to ChatGPT, which "would defeat the whole purpose"; validation simulated thousands of conversations [37:43].
- Chen: a dried blood spot card in the post gives dozens of standard biochemistry panels; phones can take vital signs from a face scan and run cognitive tests [39:58]. He said agentic AI is the newer use, machine learning the original one [39:58].
- Manor on Taya's limits: it knows only what users tell it; people on many medications, pregnant or with a complicated chronic condition should consult a healthcare provider [45:08]. Shoppers should ask who built a tool, on what data, and whether it can explain its answers [47:08].
- Chen: the stated public position of OpenAI and Anthropic is that paid or sponsored content does not go into model training or chat answers; he called healthcare the "golden goose" for AI companies [48:37].
- Spagnuolo on personalisation: coffee was once said to raise and later to lower heart-attack risk, until caffeine metabolism explained the difference; wide individual responses sit behind meta-analysis averages [50:44].

summary.Summary:
Nick Morgan of Nutrition Integrated opened the day with a state of the market. Sports nutrition is obviously going mainstream, he said, but is it growing beyond the motivations that defined it, is it winning consumers while losing its identity, and is the market growing or are its boundaries just moving?

He answered with three rules. Growth does not guarantee value: whey protein prices have never been higher, and brands are going through a structural reset, cutting promotions, shrinking packs, reformulating, launching whey hybrids and trying to sell more higher-margin lines such as creatine and electrolytes. Relevance does not guarantee ownership: creatine is now for everyone, in gummies, chocolate and products for women, and hydration has no agreed formula and new leaders. Opportunity does not guarantee advantage: his company tracks 16,412 product listings in eight categories, and only a few products will succeed, by pulling on format, brand, dose, science and branded ingredients.

His conclusion was that the principles of sports nutrition have gone mainstream, not sports nutrition itself. Brands should think beyond the category, stay true to the industry's DNA, choose where to compete and know their right to win. Everyone has a seat at the table, but not everyone will win.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Starbucks' 15 g protein cold foam is his example of the bigger market: Starbucks say one in seven coffees now provides 15 g of protein. A bigger market is not more of the same market [00:00].
- Brands are not just mitigating whey prices but going through a "structural reset". New products that cut whey reliance and a shift into creatine, energy and fibre are the "top priority for brands" [00:00] (photo 6).
- More "whey hybrids" (sold as whey, blended with milk, soy or yeast to cut cost) launched in the last 12 months than ever; whey milkshakes and whey plus collagen are the next pillars [00:00] (photo 9).
- Plant protein still underdelivers on taste. It should sell itself as a very good protein, not as plant [00:00] (photo 10).
- Gummies are the fastest-growing creatine format by new launches: 8.0% of creatine products, 36.2% of them added in the last six months, with "lots of conjecture about stability" [00:00] (photo 14).
- A quarter of creatine products use a branded ingredient, most of it from one supplier, and he said there is a race to follow; pre-workout is highest at 53% [18:50] (photo 27).

Multiplier), 750 mg (Hunter & Gather), 1,000 mg (LMNT). 69% of powders include four or five electrolytes; 8% claim Himalayan sea salt as a natural sodium source. The slide: "there is no optimal formula" [00:00] (photo 18).
- Hydration powders are positioned three ways: everyday (Humantra, Hunter & Gather, Repowr: routine, natural, sugar-free), superior (SOS "4x faster than water", Ancient + Brave, ARTAH "cellular hydration") and performance (226ERS Hydra Zero on sweat losses, HIGH5 Isotonic carbs plus electrolytes, Precision PH strength options) (photo 22).
- Naturalness: 40% state natural colours, 46% use natural flavours, 43% include stevia. Humantra names grape skin as its colour source, Liquid I.V. declares sugar alongside steviol glycosides, ViDrate covers flavour, colour and sweetening in one proposition, Cadence extends the absence message to fillers [00:00] (photo 24).
- Tracked listings (US and Europe, 16,412 across eight spaces): creatine 3,448 (new-product activity +10% over the latest six months), magnesium 2,833 (+15%), collagen 2,648, energy and focus 2,153, pre-workout 1,869, sleep and mood 1,626, electrolyte 1,487, longevity 348 (+20% new). From the stage: almost 3,500 creatine, almost 2,800 magnesium, over 2,500 collagen. "Only a few will be really successful" [00:00] (photo 23).
- Branded ingredient penetration (share of tracked products with at least one identified branded ingredient): pre-workout 53% (many use more than one), longevity 40%, energy and focus 31%, sleep and mood 25%, creatine 25%, collagen 25%, electrolyte 17%, magnesium 17%. The slide adds that minerals in general are "needing to work harder to prove the benefit" [18:50] (photo 27).
- Longevity takes three approaches: alter the ageing process (cellular health, mitochondria, senescence), optimise the ageing experience (muscle and mobility, cognition, energy, sleep) or personalise to a life stage (ageing athletes, menopause, later life). Example: Cellaro's Vitalize AM, Renew PM and Reset monthly range against the 12 hallmarks of ageing [18:50] (photo 29).
- Longevity and athlete-backed brands compete for the same consumer: Sergio Ramos links sport to longevity through Centenarian ("Real longevity, backed by science. To perform better. To live better."), with normal sports products framed as living better today. The competitive set has never been broader [18:50] (photo 30).
- Brands should engage with gut and microbiome, longevity and GLP-1, but stay true to the industry's DNA; this will be "the biggest challenge you face for your budgets and strategy in 2027 and beyond" [18:50].
- The four closing principles: think beyond the category (new consumers, needs and occasions); stay true to your DNA (capabilities, credibility, differentiation); choose where to compete ("where you could play from where you should play"); know your right to win (where you can create distinctive value). "Growth creates opportunity. Understanding change creates advantage." [18:50] (photo 32)

Hydration powders are positioned three ways: everyday (Humantra, Hunter & Gather, Repowr: routine, natural, sugar-free), superior (SOS "4x faster than water", Ancient + Brave, ARTAH "cellular hydration") and performance (226ERS Hydra Zero on sweat losses, HIGH5 Isotonic carbs plus electrolytes, Precision PH strength options) (photo 22).

Naturalness: 40% state natural colours, 46% use natural flavours, 43% include stevia. Humantra names grape skin as its colour source, Liquid I.V. declares sugar alongside steviol glycosides, ViDrate covers flavour, colour and sweetening in one proposition, Cadence extends the absence message to fillers [00:00] (photo 24).

Tracked listings (US and Europe, 16,412 across eight spaces): creatine 3,448 (new-product activity +10% over the latest six months), magnesium 2,833 (+15%), collagen 2,648, energy and focus 2,153, pre-workout 1,869, sleep and mood 1,626, electrolyte 1,487, longevity 348 (+20% new). From the stage: almost 3,500 creatine, almost 2,800 magnesium, over 2,500 collagen. "Only a few will be really successful" [00:00] (photo 23).

Branded ingredient penetration (share of tracked products with at least one identified branded ingredient): pre-workout 53% (many use more than one), longevity 40%, energy and focus 31%, sleep and mood 25%, creatine 25%, collagen 25%, electrolyte 17%, magnesium 17%. The slide adds that minerals in general are "needing to work harder to prove the benefit" [18:50] (photo 27).

Longevity takes three approaches: alter the ageing process (cellular health, mitochondria, senescence), optimise the ageing experience (muscle and mobility, cognition, energy, sleep) or personalise to a life stage (ageing athletes, menopause, later life). Example: Cellaro's Vitalize AM, Renew PM and Reset monthly range against the 12 hallmarks of ageing [18:50] (photo 29).

Longevity and athlete-backed brands compete for the same consumer: Sergio Ramos links sport to longevity through Centenarian ("Real longevity, backed by science. To perform better. To live better."), with normal sports products framed as living better today. The competitive set has never been broader [18:50] (photo 30).

Brands should engage with gut and microbiome, longevity and GLP-1, but stay true to the industry's DNA; this will be "the biggest challenge you face for your budgets and strategy in 2027 and beyond" [18:50].

The four closing principles: think beyond the category (new consumers, needs and occasions); stay true to your DNA (capabilities, credibility, differentiation); choose where to compete ("where you could play from where you should play"); know your right to win (where you can create distinctive value). "Growth creates opportunity. Understanding change creates advantage." [18:50] (photo 32)

items.title: Unfiltered: An Insider's View of the Whey Protein Market

speakers.name: Alan Johnstone
speakers.role: Owner (as introduced; formerly Arla Foods Ingredients)

items.to_check: His first employer, which Otter heard as "Sarawak International"; the price source behind the euro per kilogram figures; the chair (Speaker 1) is unnamed by Otter.
items.added_by: Claude (from the event app's programme, screenshots from Nathan at 11:39-11:40 on 9 Nov 2026)

summary.Summary:
Alan Johnstone, who has spent most of the last decades selling whey protein, most recently at Arla Foods Ingredients, and now runs Nutrilution, explained why whey prices hit records this year and what buyers should do about it.

His answer starts with milk. Whey protein comes from cheese, and cheese production grows only about one and a half percent a year, while demand for whey protein grows by 10% or more: sports nutrition, GLP-1 users, protein in everyday food, and clear whey. Filtration plants are expensive and take years to build, and producers have put the whey they have into isolate, so concentrate was short when brands had just switched to it.

Prices then swing further than supply and demand alone would explain, because buyers stock up when prices rise and wait when they fall. That is happening now: concentrate is falling fast, isolate is correcting, and the proteins brands moved into are rising.

His advice was plain. Do not try to time the bottom. Keep buying steadily if today's price lets you make money. And accept that whey will stay expensive, because the supply limit is structural.
summary.Key takeaways:
- The core constraint: cheese production grows about 1.5% a year, while whey protein demand grows over 10%. He called it the most important conclusion of the talk [00:16] (photo 7).
- Producers chose isolate. Over five years WPI grew 15.0% a year and WPC80 1.5%; clear WPI is now about a quarter of all isolate (photo 9).
- Between 25 August and 4 November 2026, WPC80 fell 40.7% to €16.00/kg and WPI 20.3% to €25.50/kg, while MPC85 rose 13.5% to €15.80/kg (photo 18).
- New capacity will not close the gap: he forecast WPI at 7 to 11% a year and WPC80 at 4 to 7% to 2030, and both cannot reach the top of their range [00:16] (photo 11).
- Mainstream buyers choose on taste and texture, not protein source, and whey is the easiest protein to make taste good [00:16].
- For buyers: "Don't try to time the market. Keep inventory steady. Whey will be expensive." (photo 20)
summary.For Vita Actives:
- The structural case for non-dairy protein comes from a whey insider: supply is capped by cheese and he expects whey to stay expensive [00:16]. My reading: this is the opening for IsoClr: Pea.
- He also set the bar. Mainstream consumers care about taste and texture, not source [00:16]. My reading: a clear pea isolate has to win on taste and clarity before it wins on supply.
- Clear whey is almost all WPI, where supply is tightest (photo 9). My reading: a clear pea isolate is positioned exactly there.
- Brands have just reformulated and are reviewing protein blends while WPC80 falls (photo 18). My reading: now is the time to be in front of formulators, before WPC80 settles.
summary.Quotes:
- "...certainly the more mainstream you get with protein products, the less people care about the protein source. I think what people always care about is taste and texture. And whey protein is delicious." Speaker 2 (Alan Johnstone) [00:16]
- "...if WPI is growing 11% a year, then WPC 80 has to be more like four because there's not enough whey." Speaker 2 (Alan Johnstone) [00:16]
- "So over the last few weeks, WPC80 has been falling pretty hard. WPI still expensive, but definitely correcting." Speaker 2 (Alan Johnstone) [00:16]
- "...whey protein will be expensive. It should be expensive. It's the best protein source for so many uses. It's got a structural supply restriction, and the amount of protein is not really going away." Speaker 2 (Alan Johnstone) [00:16]
summary.Follow-ups:
- Talk to Alan Johnstone (Nutrilution) about his price series and the capacity lists; he invited conversations on sourcing strategy [00:16].
- His price series is Vesper's; check whether we have access, or want it (photo 2).
- Check the Euromonitor figure he cited for sports nutrition growth, 10% a year; his slide says 8 to 10% [00:16] (photo 3).
summary.Key slides:
- (photo 7) Supply bottlenecks: cheese production +1.5% a year against whey protein demand of 10%+.
- (photo 9) Five years of supply growth: WPI the growth engine, clear WPI a quarter of all isolate.
- (photo 18) The last ten weeks: WPC80 and WPI falling while MPC85 rises to meet WPC80.
- (photo 20) Where prices go from here, with his three takeaways for buyers.
summary.Detail:
- Prices this year: WPI went from around €7/kg in 2023 to over €30/kg; WPC80 held around €12/kg, then rose to €28/kg in about six weeks. WPC80 was the bigger risk for brands because they had already moved their sourcing into it [00:16].
- The price chart (Vesper, EU monthly, December 2019 to October 2026): WPC80 about €5/kg in 2020 and 2023, peaking about €12 in 2022 and about €26 to 27 in mid 2026; WPI about €8 in 2020, €18 in 2022, €7 in 2023 and about €31 in mid 2026. The slide headline: "Record highs this summer (WPC80 up roughly 6x since 2020, WPI near €32/kg), now correcting" (photo 2).
- Demand drivers: traditional sports nutrition at 10% a year on Euromonitor, which he thinks underestimates it; GLP-1 users as new demand; protein going mainstream (Starbucks, Papa John's, Dunkin'); and clear whey, which barely existed five years ago and is almost all whey [00:16].
- The demand slide: the 2024 global sports nutrition market splits 48% protein powders, 26% protein bars, 17% non-protein and 9% protein RTD, growing 8 to 10% a year; clear whey SKUs are up 35% a year; 12% of US adults take a GLP-1 medication, with protein spend up 20% (KFF 2025, BCG 2026) (photo 3).
- Milk by weight: water 87.3%, lactose 4.7%, fat 3.9%, casein 2.8%, minerals 0.7%, whey protein 0.6% [00:16] (photo 4).
- The route from milk: cheese keeps the casein and fat; liquid whey goes through ultrafiltration and drying to WPC (35 to 80% protein), microfiltration or ion exchange to WPI (90% or more), then acidification or hydrolysis to clear or hydrolysed WPI. Sweet whey powder (about 12% protein), permeate, lactose, demineralised whey (D70, D90 for infant nutrition) and whey cream are the other outlets for the same whey [00:16] (photo 4).
- Three bottlenecks: factories ("CAPEX intensive, less flexible than people expect, takes years to start commercial production"), liquid whey, and by-products, "a major influencer of producer value"; WPI makers must also sell a fatty protein stream [00:16] (photo 6) (photo 7).
- Global production: WPC80 334,000 t in 2020 and 360,000 t in 2025; WPI 80,494 t and 161,800 t; total 414,494 t and 521,800 t, up 26% (4.7% a year). Clear WPI was 40,450 t in 2025, which he said is the top of the estimate range; standard WPI grew 8.6% a year, below the category [00:16] (photo 8) (photo 9).
- Announced US capacity (McCully Consulting, approximate): 24,400 t of WPC80 and 7,500 t of WPI in 2026, 41,600 t and 20,300 t in 2027, 45,900 t and 22,900 t in 2028. UK, EU and Oceania: FrieslandCampina (WPI), Fonterra (speciality) and Polmlek (WPC, WPI) in 2026; Tirlán (WPC, WPI, clear) and Liprovit (WPI) in 2027; Arla's mozzarella plant in 2028. He said the European list is incomplete [00:16] (photo 11).
- The buying cycle, using COVID as the example: longer lead times, more stock, rising demand, buyers competing, rising prices and an incentive to buy early; then the reverse, with the 2022 peak as logistics freed up and buyers destocked, and the 2023 trough as buyers waited with stocks too low [00:16] (photo 13) (photo 14) (photo 15).
- Now: new US plants planned three or four years ago are commissioning; isolate, WPC35 and sweet whey powder are better uses of whey, so WPC80 output should fall; substitutes (MPC85, MPI, caseins, plant proteins) are rising, and WPC80 and milk protein "should never meet" [00:16].
- Weekly Vesper prices, 25 August to 4 November 2026: WPC80 €27.00 to €16.00; WPI €32.00 to €25.50; MPC85 €13.92 to €15.80 (photo 16) (photo 18).
- Forces for the next move. WPC80, up: strong other derivatives, rising alternatives, long-term protein demand; down: high inventories, powerful momentum, demand destruction. WPI, up: smaller share of brand costs, healthy inventories on both sides, harder to replace; down: demand destruction, production increases due (photo 16).
- Where prices go: "structurally rising but volatile"; the correction "may overshoot below trend" before demand pulls prices back up. The slide says the trend and forward path are "directional, not a forecast" (photo 19).
- He quoted Keynes, that markets can stay irrational longer than you can stay solvent, so WPC80 and MPC85 touching does not mean they part at once, "but it can't go on forever" [00:16].
- Nutrilution sells niche, higher-value ingredients and advises buyers on whey and dairy protein sourcing, including cross-continental supply chains [00:16].
