items.title: Clicks to Community: Turning Digital Engagement into Brand Loyalty

speakers.name: Dan Richardson
speakers.role: Nutritionist (as he described himself; works across professional sport)

items.to_check: The recording starts mid-sentence (the chair's opening is cut); Otter's speaker labels are my reading (Speaker 1 Nikki Hancocks, 2 Sinead Gibbons, 3 Julian Harvie, 4 Dan Richardson) and the [14:35] turn merges the chair's question with Sinead's answer; Speaker 5 ([18:28]) is unidentified; Luca's "Digital Finance Act" is as transcribed; whether photos of the slides exist (if any were used).
items.added_by: Claude (from the event app's programme, screenshots from Nathan at 11:39-11:40 on 9 Nov 2026)

summary.Summary:
Nikki Hancocks of NutraIngredients chaired a panel on how brands build communities online while regulators watch. She opened with a report of more than 1,000 misleading food posts by influencers, with supplements the most frequent subject.

The panel agreed that social content works when it educates or entertains rather than sells. Sinead Gibbons said almost none of Tonic Health's content is about its products; its supermarket swap videos have built 1.9 million followers. Julian Harvie said AG1 learned that talking about its trials and testing did not land, so it keeps the science further down the funnel and practises restraint; Clearcast rejected three versions of its TV advert's opening line. Dan Richardson, a nutritionist in professional sport, said athletes want the headline backed by research, that brands slip by using buzzwords whose meaning differs from the research, and that athletes are the most impressionable audience of all.

Luca Bucchini, speaking for ESSNA, set out the rules and the failures he sees most: undisclosed ads, and marketing strategies built around non-compliance. Brands carry most of the responsibility for what their influencers claim. On AI, Julian's rule is that every idea begins and ends with a human; Luca expects regulators to act as people take nutrition advice from AI.
summary.Key takeaways:
- More than 1,000 misleading food posts by influencers were counted in a recent report, with supplements the most frequent subject [00:01].
- Tonic runs itself as "a media business that happens to sell vitamins": 99% of its content is not about its products, and it has 1.9 million followers and about 70 million views a month [01:00], [03:24].
- AG1 found that talking about trials and third-party testing did not land: "people didn't care". Too much evidence fails at the top of the funnel; the science sits mid-funnel [04:17], [18:30].
- Clearcast rejected "the best version of you", "a better version of you" and "a slightly better version of you" before approving "Ever wondered what life would be like with a little extra help?" Julian's lesson: "creative constraint is a very powerful way to deliver better communication" [18:30].
- Brands bear most responsibility for their influencers' health claims in most jurisdictions; the answer is training, contracts and briefing [28:27].
- Athletes are "probably the most impressionable group": they believe a claim of "up to 10% better performance" applies to them personally [32:33].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Our customers' marketing teams are under claims pressure from the ASA, Clearcast and the claims regulation, and the panel's answer was education that does not sell: "what is creatine, how does it work" is exactly what AG1 makes with its experts [22:46].
- My reading: a branded ingredient earns its place by giving brands substantiated, claim-safe education they can publish, in the headline-plus-evidence form Dan described, not by giving them stronger claims [06:30].
- For CreaWin, Dan's food-first framing and his athlete stories show creatine is already a mainstay for athletes and nutritionists [24:22], [32:33]. My reading: our creatine content should be calm and educational, and wording we supply to brands must survive an ASA review.
- Brands carry the liability for what influencers say [28:27]. My reading: they will want suppliers' claims referenced and hedged exactly.
- Relevance medium: marketing and regulation, adjacent to our ingredients.
summary.Quotes:
- "...99% of our content is not about our product, which a lot of people on our board and you know investors constantly question every day." Speaker 2 (Sinead Gibbons) [03:24]
- "...we talk a lot about restraint being its own version of power in our space, where so many businesses oversell and underdeliver, and we we actively pursue the opposite dynamic." Speaker 3 (Julian Harvie) [18:30]
- "The first is that it's not when a brand occasionally oversteps, but where there is a marketing strategy, it builds around non-compliance." Luca Buccini (ESSNA) [11:59]
- "I think athletes probably one of the most impressionable audiences because it's all about a competitive edge and advantage." Speaker 4 (Dan Richardson) [32:33]
summary.Follow-ups:
- Find the NutraIngredients report on the more than 1,000 misleading influencer posts [00:01].
- Luca Bucchini (ESSNA): the upcoming digital act he named (Otter: "Digital Finance Act"), and ESSNA's position on influencer responsibility [09:45], [28:27].
- Dan Richardson (DRN Nutrition Group) works across professional sport and academies and is food first on creatine; a possible contact on how clubs see creatine and collagen [24:22], [32:33].
- Tonic Health's AI compliance review and AG1's "Dropping Hours" series as examples of compliant education content [14:35], [04:17].
summary.Detail:
- Tonic's flagship content is the "Unsponsored Truth": its founder gives simple supermarket swaps. Clips are 20 to 30 seconds, three posts a day; people come to social "to be educated or to be entertained" [01:00], [03:24].
- Tonic posts 900 pieces of content a month across four channels with one 22-year-old social media manager and a freelance editor. After the ASA pulled up a profile cover for its magnesium drink ("...she wrote on the social cover the best sleep supplement in the market, and now we don't have that claim"), every piece now goes through an AI compliance agent [14:35].
- Tonic never deletes a challenged post: it changes the caption, answers the comments, sends voice notes and makes response videos, because "trust is really built in those small moments" [14:35].
- Julian: on social, people "come to be educated or entertained", and education must be hyper relevant to the person; "Too much evidence doesn't work." AG1's US campaign "WTF is NSF" and its "Dropping Hours" series humanise the science without selling [04:17].
- AG1 cannot associate healthcare professionals, dietitians or doctors directly with the brand, so it uses them for pure education ("what is creatine? Like, how does it work?", "why is magnesium important?") and hopes the credibility transfers [22:46].
- Dan: athletes want the headline, backed by the research. The common slip is swapping dull research words for buzzwords whose connotations differ, often "genuine accidental misleading"; "what you can and can't say around a product is a massive gray area" [06:30], [08:33].
- Dan is food first: on a creatine company's podcast he said not everybody should take creatine until the baseline of nutrition is fixed, and the company objected [24:22].
- A 35-year-old EFL player with 200-plus appearances bought a supplement off TikTok Shop; athletes think they are the subject of the research papers [32:33].
- Luca's rules: the nutrition and health claims regulation, the UK advertising codes, member state influencer rules, and a new digital act whose text is not yet known (Otter: "Digital Finance Act") [09:45].
- Luca's recurring failures: undisclosed ads, no training or allocated responsibility with creators, strategies built around non-compliance, and following a non-compliant discourse [11:59].
- Provocation without a solution is fearmongering: Tonic will not post a call-out unless it gives the healthier swap [30:18].
- AI: Julian's hard rule is that "...the idea has to begin and end with a human being"; AI scales the middle, and he found human copy still better by some margin [35:43]. Luca expects regulatory action as consumers take nutrition advice from AI agents [38:28]. The chair added that AI is also used to monitor posts [39:48].

Julian: on social, people "come to be educated or entertained", and education must be hyper relevant to the person; "Too much evidence doesn't work." AG1's US campaign "WTF is NSF" and its "Dropping Hours" series humanise the science without selling [04:17].

AG1 cannot associate healthcare professionals, dietitians or doctors directly with the brand, so it uses them for pure education ("what is creatine? Like, how does it work?", "why is magnesium important?") and hopes the credibility transfers [22:46].

Dan: athletes want the headline, backed by the research. The common slip is swapping dull research words for buzzwords whose connotations differ, often "genuine accidental misleading"; "what you can and can't say around a product is a massive gray area" [06:30], [08:33].
Dan is food first: on a creatine company's podcast he said not everybody should take creatine until the baseline of nutrition is fixed, and the company objected [24:22].
A 35-year-old EFL player with 200-plus appearances bought a supplement off TikTok Shop; athletes think they are the subject of the research papers [32:33].

Luca's rules: the nutrition and health claims regulation, the UK advertising codes, member state influencer rules, and a new digital act whose text is not yet known (Otter: "Digital Finance Act") [09:45].
Luca's recurring failures: undisclosed ads, no training or allocated responsibility with creators, strategies built around non-compliance, and following a non-compliant discourse [11:59].
Provocation without a solution is fearmongering: Tonic will not post a call-out unless it gives the healthier swap [30:18].

AI: Julian's hard rule is that "...the idea has to begin and end with a human being"; AI scales the middle, and he found human copy still better by some margin [35:43]. Luca expects regulatory action as consumers take nutrition advice from AI agents [38:28]. The chair added that AI is also used to monitor posts [39:48].

items.title: Fuelling the female runner: from paper to podium to partnerships
items.to_check: The recording starts mid-sentence, so the opening of the talk (and any cycling data he refers back to) is missing; the female runners paper is in peer review and not yet citable; the Nike event Otter heard as "After Doctor" is After Dark (my reading).

summary.Summary:
James Morton of Science in Sport asked whether women need to fuel differently from men when they run. His answer: the barrier is knowledge, not biology.

He started with glycogen. In a 2021 study of recreational runners, women began with less muscle glycogen than men but finished equally depleted. The gap came from dosing per kilogram of body weight: given the same absolute carbohydrate, women store about the same.

He then showed an England Athletics study of elite runners fed 60, 90 or 120 g of carbohydrate an hour over two hours near race pace. At 120 g the switch from carbohydrate to fat never came, in men or in women. Both sexes oxidised the extra carbohydrate equally well, and running economy improved by two to 3%. Women reported more gut symptoms, so tolerance may differ slightly, but oxidation does not.

From this he drew a framework that sets carbohydrate by intensity and duration, up to 120 g an hour for a marathon, and described SiS's partnership with Nike's After Dark Tour as an education programme rather than a product launch. His conclusion: female runners do not know the numbers and have lived with under-fuelling. Treat the female athlete as an athlete first, and fuel for the work, not the menstrual cycle.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Women started with less muscle glycogen than men but finished similarly depleted. The gap was under 5 g in the gastrocnemius, comes from dosing per kilogram, and has no practical bearing on guidelines [00:00].
- At 120 g of carbohydrate an hour, the crossover from carbohydrate to fat was completely prevented over two hours, in both sexes; at 60 g it came after about an hour [00:00] (photo 4) (photo 6).
- Men and women oxidise carbohydrate taken during exercise at comparable rates, rising with dose (120 > 90 > 60 g); at 120 g some individuals oxidised 80 to 100 percent of what they took [00:00] (photo 7).
- Running economy improved by two to 3% at 120 g an hour, against the 4% Nike claimed for the Vaporfly; he is "pretty sure" this is part of why running records are falling [00:00] (photo 9).
- Women reported more gastrointestinal symptoms, "which may be due to anatomical differences in colon length"; individual variation warrants personalised fuelling [00:00] (photo 9).
- The biggest barrier is educational, in a world where under-fuelling has been prevalent; he does not believe in fuelling to the menstrual cycle [00:00] (photo 20).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Nothing in the talk touches our ingredients. No protein, creatine or pre-workout was mentioned from the stage; the only protein on a slide is 25 g (including 5 g collagen) in the two Run Recovery drinks of the Nike x SiS range, source not stated (photo 19).
- The value is customer insight. SiS builds its pitch on its own trials (England Athletics, Nike), published papers and a one-slide framework, and its chief science voice is openly sceptical of claims he sees on social media [00:00] (photo 12). My reading: a brand like this expects a supplier to bring trial data and a one-slide rule of thumb, not a benefit list; CreaWin and IsoClr: Pea material should meet that standard.
- Gut tolerance (more symptoms in women at high intakes, a runner skipping gels on an unhappy stomach) is adjacent to the digestibility story for a clear pea protein (photo 15) (my reading).
- The clear recovery drinks carry 25 g protein in a clear format for women runners, which is the format IsoClr: Pea is made for (photo 19) (my reading).
- Relevance low: carbohydrate fuelling, outside our range.

summary.Detail:
- The 2021 study (Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise): recreational runners with muscle biopsies before and after three sessions, on 6 g per kg carbohydrate on the day, a 10-mile run at lactate threshold, 8 x 800 m and 3 x 10 minutes [00:00].
- Given the same absolute carbohydrate, "there isn't really any differences in glycogen storage", even if women then take eight or nine grams per kilogram. His hedge: for a given relative intake women "may present with slightly less absolute glycogen" [00:00].
- The elite study: men with marathon bests about 2:20, women about 2:40. 8 g per kg carbohydrate on day one, a 2 g per kg breakfast on day two, then 15 minutes at 95% of lactate threshold, 90 minutes at 94% of lactate turnpoint (simulated race pace) and 15 minutes at 95% of lactate threshold. The 60 g an hour condition was maltodextrin only; 90 and 120 g were 1:1 maltodextrin and fructose [00:00] (photo 2). The male data is Ravikanti et al. (2025), Journal of Applied Physiology; the female data is under revision [00:00].
- Crossover: at 60 g an hour, after about 60 minutes (the slides show about 60 to 75 minutes in both sexes); 90 g shifted it right; 120 g prevented it for the full two hours. Men's carbohydrate oxidation on 120 g held at about 3.0 to 3.2 g a minute from 45 to 105 minutes [00:00] (photo 3) (photo 4) (photo 6).
- Exogenous oxidation (carbon-13): about 1 g a minute at 60 g an hour, close to 1.3 to 1.4 at 90 g, and at 120 g "some of the highest rates of oxidation ever reported in literature". Peak means read from the chart: men about 1.0, 1.5 and 1.8 g a minute at 60, 90 and 120 g; women about 1.0, 1.45 and 1.75; seven to eight participants a group [00:00] (photo 7).
- The conclusion slide: "Female trained runners can oxidise exogenous CHO at comparable rates to male runners. Furthermore, in both sexes, 120 g/h maintains whole body CHO oxidation, CHO dependency and reduces the oxygen cost of running (i.e. improves running economy) compared with traditional CHO guidelines of 60-90 g/h. However, individual variations in rates of exogenous CHO oxidation and gastrointestinal symptoms warrant CHO personalisation strategies." (photo 9)
- Women may differ slightly in their ability to tolerate carbohydrate at those intensities; there is "definitely not a difference" in their ability to digest and oxidise it [00:00].
- The fuelling matrix (Journal of Nutrition): an easy 60-minute run needs no carbohydrate; 60 minutes at higher intensity 30 to 60 g an hour; team sport or half marathon towards 90 g; two to three hours a definite rationale for 120 g. Ultra-endurance (three to eight hours) is the gap SiS's science strategy will work on [00:00].
- The framework in full (Morton et al. 2026, Journal of Nutrition) plots intensity (zones 1 to 5; moderate under 2 mmol/L, heavy 2 to 4, severe over 4) against duration: under an hour, 0 g, 0 to 30 g or 30 to 60 g single source for HIT (mouth rinse, drinks, gels); one to two hours, 30 to 60 g single source, 60 to 90 g single or dual source for soccer, 90 g dual source for a half marathon (drinks, gels, chews); two to three hours, 60 to 90 g single or dual, 90 to 120 g dual, 120 g dual source for a marathon (drinks, gels, chews, bars); beyond three hours cycling stages, beyond six ultra (photo 10) (photo 12).
- The barriers: female marathoners "do not know the numbers" (psychological capability; participant 18 took her first gel at 7 or 8 miles and went by what others do), and tolerating carbohydrate in a race can be a barrier (physical capability; participant 13 aimed for about 80 g an hour, felt her stomach "was not happy" in the heat and skipped her last two gels). Like men, female runners need to practise fuelling in training (photo 13) (photo 14) (photo 15).
- Nike's After Dark Tour runs women's night races in seven cities. SiS partnered on education rather than product creation, with co-branded products by race duration; the partnership continues [00:00]. The Sydney 21K race pack sells at $40.00 ("Fuel your night"): eight packs of Run Fuel Endurance energy gels (3 x 60 ml), Run Hydro+ electrolyte powder (4.3 g), a Run Fuel Endurance energy chew (50 g) and Run Recovery Endurance powder (73 g) (photo 17) (photo 18).
- The Nike x SiS After Dark range, "designed for her", laid out for 10K and half marathon: Run Fuel Isotonic gel (22 g single-source carbohydrate; before and during), Run Fuel Endurance gel (40 g dual source; during), Run Fuel Endurance chew (40 g dual source, 1:0.8 glucose to fructose; before and during), Run Hydro+ sugar-free electrolytes (350 mg sodium; before, during and after), Run Recovery (25 g single-source carbohydrate, 25 g protein including 5 g collagen; after) and Run Recovery Endurance (40 g dual-source carbohydrate, 25 g protein including 5 g collagen; after) (photo 19).
- The closing slide: "The biggest barrier to fuelling the female runner is not likely a biological limitation i.e. their gut or their muscles. Rather, it is lack of knowledge and awareness of the guidelines (i.e. educational) and the associated physiological and performance benefits, especially when considering a world where under-fuelling has been prevalent. Fuelling is less about hormones and tailoring to the menstrual cycle, put simply, it is about fuelling for the work required." (photo 20) From the stage he added that he does not believe in day-of-cycle fuelling at all, and treats a female athlete as an athlete first [00:00].
- Q&A: nine participants gives 80% power because a 30 g step changes oxidation by 0.3 to 0.4 g a minute [22:54]. Women should probably be dosed per kilogram of fat-free mass, but it is hard to measure: "I'd rather be in the approximately right count than the precisely wrong count." [23:48] Dual source is needed at 90 and 120 g, above about 90 minutes, but not below, and lowers oxidation at 60 g [24:34], [25:17].

items.title: Whey & Collagen: The Protein Power Couple

speakers.name: Tess Plaquet
speakers.role: Technical sport manager (as she introduced herself)

items.to_check: Sponsored slot (Rousselot by Darling Ingredients logo on the programme). Otter produced no summary and labelled the speaker "Speaker unknown"; the recording ends mid-sentence in her closing invitation to the roundtables, so any Q&A is missing; Otter heard her name as "Staske" and Olivia Haslam introduced her as "Tess Plackett", so the spelling is unconfirmed; the currency of the "5.7 k" to "almost 32 k" a tonne WPC80 figure was not said; whether photos of the slides exist (the launch, price and study charts were on slides).

summary.Summary:
Tess Plaquet, technical sport manager at Rousselot, argued that brands should stop asking when whey prices will fall and work around them by blending whey with collagen.

She began with the market. Whey launches keep growing, and she said the forces behind whey prices, from GLP-1 users and China to whey being a cheese by-product and rising energy and labour costs, mean high prices are here to stay. Brands can raise prices, shrink packs or reformulate; she called smarter formulation with protein blends the most elegant answer. Launches combining whey and collagen are growing at almost 17.5% a year, and collagen comes from four animal sources with far steadier prices.

She then made the case that the two proteins complement rather than compete: whey builds and repairs muscle, while Rousselot's Peptan collagen peptides support tendons, joints and bone. Her evidence was Rousselot's own studies. The central one gave 22 men either 45 g of whey or 25 g of whey plus 20 g of Peptan for three weeks of training, and recovery and performance were similar in both groups. Studies of Peptan on its own reported less muscle soreness, fewer blood endotoxins after a run, better knee comfort and better sleep.

The recording ends as she invites the room to Rousselot's roundtables.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Brands have three responses to whey costs: raise the price, shrinkflation, or smarter formulation with protein blends, which she called the most elegant and a way to stand out on shelf [00:10].
- Launches combining whey and collagen are growing at almost 17.5 percent a year; a 10 g collagen plus 10 g whey product was her example [00:10].
- Collagen supply is spread across bovine, porcine, chicken and fish, and its historical prices fluctuate far less than whey's [00:10].
- Whey and collagen are "no competitors": whey for muscle, Peptan (rich in hydroxyproline, glycine and proline) for ligaments, tendons, joints and bone [00:10].
- In 22 men over three weeks of training, 25 g whey plus 20 g Peptan gave the same recovery and performance as 45 g whey [00:10].
- 20 g Peptan with vitamin C for seven days gave 28% less muscle soreness and 13% faster muscle recovery than placebo after 150 jumps [00:10].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Rousselot sells into the same brand problem we do, with a different answer: replace part of the whey with collagen, backed by a head-to-head showing no loss of recovery or performance at 25 g whey plus 20 g Peptan [00:10]. My reading: IsoClr: Pea competes for the same "smarter formulation" slot in a brand's protein review, and our pitch should match hers in form: the supply argument first, then evidence that a blend performs.
- We have no head-to-head of this kind for pea; that is the gap (my reading).
- Her collagen supply story (four animal sources, little volatility) is the kind of supply-security argument a plant protein can make more strongly (my reading).
- Nick Morgan named whey plus collagen clear drinks earlier; a clear pea plus collagen format is a possible combination rather than a competition (my reading).
- The health claims here come from Rousselot's own studies, with her hedges; none are ours. Relevance high: protein blends and whey pricing.

- "...there are more and more launches of products combining whey and collagen, so steady increase over the last couple of years, and yeah, actually an average growth rate of 17.5 percent almost." Speaker unknown (Tess Plaquet) [00:10]
- "...these two are no competitors; these two already complementary, and when you add in both, you can have extra additional health benefits." Speaker unknown (Tess Plaquet) [00:10]
- "So actually, the athletes, the recovery was the same, the performance was the same, but you also have more support in your movement system..." Speaker unknown (Tess Plaquet) [00:10]
summary.Follow-ups:
- Ask Rousselot for the published papers behind the five Peptan studies (whey against whey plus Peptan; soreness; endotoxins; knee; sleep) and the whey plus collagen launch data [00:10].
- Her WPC80 price (5.7k a tonne in 2023 to almost 32k in 2026, currency not given) differs from Alan Johnstone's Vesper series (WPC80 about €5/kg in 2023 and €27.00/kg on 25 August 2026, unfiltered-an-insider-s-view-of): ask Rousselot for the source and currency, and note both views until it is clear [00:10].
- Confirm the speaker's name spelling (programme: Tess Plaquet; introduced as "Tess Plackett") [00:10].
- Question for us: what head-to-head data would show a pea isolate replacing part of the whey without loss of performance? (my reading).
summary.Detail:
- What she said about whey: launches of whey food and beverage supplements have grown steadily for two years at seven and a half percent a year; the biggest price rise was in 24 to 25, "with a growth rate of 8.7"; and "in 2023 the price of a ton of whey protein concentrate of 80% was 5.7 k, whereas in 2026 it's almost 32 k. So really, in just three years' time, it's almost a sixfold" [00:10].
- Her drivers, which she said mean "those prices will be here to stay": demand from active lifestyle consumers, GLP-1 users advised to take extra protein, and China; whey is a by-product of cheese and cannot be scaled easily; gas, electricity, labour, filtration costs, tariffs, geopolitics and climate push the same way [00:10].
- Whey is a complete protein rich in BCAAs, for muscle building and repair. Peptan is hydrolysed collagen, rich in hydroxyproline (unique to animal-derived collagen and, she said, linked to holistic health benefits), glycine and proline [00:10].
- The head-to-head: 22 men, 45 g whey against 25 g whey plus 20 g Peptan, three weeks of training, measured on jump height and creatine kinase; no difference between groups at the end [00:10].
- Soreness: 24 men, 20 g Peptan with vitamin C or placebo for seven days, then 150 jumps [00:10].
- Endotoxins: 10 g Peptan for seven days, then 45 minutes before a 70-minute run; endotoxins were the same as without exercise, while on placebo they rose. Her hedge: "...it's really an indication that taking in peptan could lessen the amount of endotoxins in your blood and could reduce your digestive discomfort" [00:10].
- Knees: women with mild knee discomfort, 8 g a day for six months; significant improvement in discomfort and function at three months, and further at six [00:10].
- Sleep: 15 g a day, polysomnography on night seven; awakenings fell from around 30 to 22, subjective sleep improved, and the Peptan group scored 100% on a Stroop test against a weaker placebo group [00:10].
- Rousselot offers roundtables on application advantages and help incorporating collagen [00:10].

summary.Summary:
Olivia Haslam of NutraIngredients talked with Ollie Marchon, founder of the UK brand Marchon, and Liam Holmes, its head of product, about what the rise of the everyday athlete means for sports nutrition.

Ollie described three kinds of consumer: those inspired by training, who want habits and to feel better; those driven by it, who measure progress and time their nutrients; and those who live by it, planning the whole day around training. Most people on Marchon's training app train at 6 in the morning, which changes what they need. Liam argued for situational formats, such as carbohydrate in a pre-workout for people who cannot eat first.

Ollie said awareness of supplements is high but understanding lags, so education, honest positioning and effective doses matter more than hype. Creatine shows how this works: decades of research and podcast voices did the selling, and it built the daily supplement habit. Liam sees creatine as here to stay and moving into cognition; for ingredient suppliers, the challenge is stability in water, gummies and other formats. Claims are a regulatory nightmare, so Marchon adds ingredients to products already in people's routines.

Asked where the category goes in five years, Liam answered: formats that improve compliance.

- Most of their 8,000 daily training-app users train at 6:00 in the morning, so Marchon put carbohydrate into a pre-workout for people who will not eat toast or porridge first [00:54], [04:00].

summary.Summary:
Morgan Griffiths of Lumina Intelligence argued that GLP-1 drugs, bad news for many food and drink brands, are an opportunity for active nutrition.

He started with scale. In the UK, 6.1% of people are taking a GLP-1 now, and with past users and those considering it the total is about 18.4 million people. Use is similar in Italy, France, Germany and Spain.

He then described the users. They are not the obesity population the drugs were designed for: most are women, Gen X or Millennial and better off. They are already health-minded and willing to pay more for quality. Most expect to spend the same or more on food and drink, and near 60% expect to take more supplements, with creatine higher on the list than he expected.

He saw three openings: side effects, nutrition gaps such as protein intake and muscle loss, and lapsed users, who risk regaining the weight because the drug changed their behaviour without them changing their habits. Huel, Cambridge Nutrition, Portion IQ and Boots are already moving, and Lumina forecasts UK use at around 11% by 2031.
summary.Key takeaways:
- In the UK, 6.1% currently take GLP-1s, 5.7% have taken them and 15.1% are considering them: together about 18.4 million people [00:08].
- Current users are not the obesity population the drugs were designed for: 56% female, 63% Gen X or Millennial, 63% ABC1, and 74% happy to pay more for quality [00:08].
- Two thirds expect to spend the same or more on food and drink, and near 60% are likely to increase their supplement use; creatine was "maybe slightly higher" than expected [00:08].
- The openings are side effects, nutrition gaps (muscle loss, difficulty eating enough protein and nutrients) and lapsed users, with a malnutrition risk for people who eat less without care [00:08].
- He cited a British Medical Association study: people are four times more likely to regain weight lost with GLP-1 than weight lost by traditional methods [00:08].
- Putting GLP-1 on pack is "a kind of a health claim", so retailer support such as Boots' GLP-1 bays matters [00:08].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- GLP-1 users are affluent, health-minded and expect to spend more on supplements, and protein and muscle loss are among their concerns [00:08]. My reading: a direct opening for IsoClr: Pea in low-volume, high-protein products, and for CreaWin, since creatine already ranks higher than expected among what users take.
- Lapsed users are his largest gap [00:08]. My reading: muscle-retention products (protein plus creatine) for people coming off the drugs are a concept to put to customers.
- Brands avoid "GLP-1" on pack and rely on retailer bays like Boots' [00:08]. My reading: supplier support should be evidence on muscle and protein, not GLP-1 wording.
- The survey covers the UK and four big EU markets, which match our customers' markets [00:08].
- Relevance high: GLP-1 nutrition and market structure.

summary.Summary:
Gulrez Zariwala, founder director of the Centre for Nutraceuticals, asked which supplements aimed at GLP-1 and appetite have science behind them.

He began with the biology. Gut hormones such as GLP-1 and PYY signal fullness, and ghrelin signals hunger. Earlier obesity drugs that acted on the brain carried psychiatric risks, which turned the field to gut hormones. GLP-1 drugs give weight loss of five to 15%, but some of what is lost is muscle.

The boom in GLP-1 supplements, he said, has brought lawsuits, regulatory clampdowns and lower consumer confidence. He then went through the candidates. Proteins have an undisputed effect on GLP-1 release. Berberine, cinnamon and bitter compounds have plausible mechanisms but modest effects and few human studies. His centre's own trials found that potato protein raised GLP-1 as much as whey protein isolate, and that a mulberry extract raised GLP-1 and reduced appetite and food noise.

His conclusion: supplements may fill a gap for current or lapsed users, but none can match a drug, so expectations need managing. Products with scientific validation increase market resilience, and GLP-1 use creates demand for proteins, fibre, probiotics and multivitamins.
summary.Key takeaways:
- GLP-1 drugs give weight loss of "between five to 15%", but users lose body weight rather than only body fat, and muscle loss "can lead to sarcopenia" [00:15].
- The GLP-1 supplement boom brought "some high-profile lawsuits", regulatory clampdowns and lower consumer confidence [00:15].
- Proteins have an "undisputed effect" on GLP-1 secretion, depending on quality and amino acid profile [00:15].
- Berberine, cinnamon and bitter compounds have mechanisms but "mild to modest" effects and few human studies [00:15].
- In his centre's appetite trial, potato protein and whey protein isolate raised GLP-1 significantly and equally [00:15].
- A mulberry extract significantly raised GLP-1 at 180 minutes and significantly reduced appetite and food noise; the paper is due to be submitted next week [00:15].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- A plant protein matched whey protein isolate on GLP-1 response in his trial; that was potato protein, not pea [00:15]. My reading: this opens a satiety angle for IsoClr: Pea, but only with our own data, and his centre runs exactly this protocol for industry partners.
- Muscle loss on GLP-1 drugs is his headline risk, and protein is the one supplement class he called validated on both satiety and muscle [00:15]. My reading: protein for GLP-1 users is a pitch with science behind it; CreaWin's place there would rest on its muscle evidence, which he did not discuss.
- His warning on overclaiming (lawsuits, clampdowns) fits EU claims rules [00:15]. My reading: we should not let customers imply GLP-1 effects for our ingredients.
- Relevance high: GLP-1 nutrition and protein.

- "So a significant increase in GLP-1, increase sorry reduction in appetite and reduction in food noise." Speaker 2 (Gulrez Zariwala) [00:15]
- "There is no natural supplement solution that can match the magnitude of response which you will get with a pharmacological drug..." Speaker 2 (Gulrez Zariwala) [00:15]
- "...products that have scientific validation increase market resilience..." Speaker 2 (Gulrez Zariwala) [00:15]

summary.Summary:
The day's last panel asked what GLP-1 means for sports and active nutrition beyond the boom. It brought together Nick Morgan of Nutrition Integrated, Brett Hamer, product director at Myprotein, and Ed Tooley, a performance nutritionist.

They agreed that GLP-1 is speeding up trends that already existed rather than creating new ones, and that few brands put GLP-1 on pack: Myprotein sells need-state bundles, and retailer bays such as Boots' let brands be present without the wording. Brett said clear protein, and clear protein with collagen, is selling very well to this consumer, while plant protein has not taken off; Nick put that down to taste. Nick called creatine almost a tier one ingredient, now bought by women, older consumers and people managing their weight.

They differed in where they looked. Ed's concern was nutrition: people who simply eat less risk missing protein, carbohydrate and micronutrients, so he puts protein first. Brett and Nick looked at products: both would launch protein with fibre, and Nick named low-volume clear protein with fibre and products for people coming off the drugs as the gaps. For the next disruptor, Brett named people coming off the drugs, Ed education between on and off, and Nick AI.

The recording ends with the host's close of the day.

items.title: Nick Morgan: how longevity is sold, from hallmarks to habits
items.to_check: The recording holds only the last six minutes of the talk, so the billed title, the speaker's organisation and role (Nutrition Integrated is not said in the recording), the five points he refers back to, and the room are unconfirmed.

summary.Summary:
The recording catches the last six minutes of Nick Morgan's talk on the longevity consumer. His question was how brands actually sell longevity, and his answer was: not through the science.

Longevity now sits inside women's health, menopause and sports nutrition. Consumers connect with "energy and vitality" and "cellular health", not the hallmarks of ageing; in about 300 products he coded, only 9% refer to the hallmarks at all. Brands sell a routine of about three products, not one, so an ingredient is sold on how it fits the customer's product system.

Longevity is also one of the most expensive categories per serve. His example was creatine: a median of about 50 cents a serve on the sports shelf, and far more with longevity on the front of the pack. A good story can turn an existing ingredient into a premium one.

He closed on where the category is going. Capsules dominate today, but formats are widening into liquids, chocolate, gummies and drinks, cellular claims are entering hydration, and longevity is moving into sports nutrition. His advice was to keep up, because what brands say today will change within months.

- Consumers buy "energy and vitality" and "cellular health"; the hallmarks of ageing are "for this people in this room" [00:00].
- Of about 300 products coded, 9% refer to the hallmarks and only 4%, he thinks, put them in lead copy [00:00].
- "You don't sell one product in 2026": brands sell a routine of about three products, and an ingredient is sold on how it fits the customer's product system [00:00].
- Longevity products are among the most expensive per serve; the creatine median is about 50 cents a serve, and the same ingredient labelled longevity can be "a hell of a lot more expensive" [00:00].

items.title: Nuritas: AI-discovered plant peptides and the PeptiStrong trials
items.to_check: Billed title, Miguel's surname (Otter heard "Miguel Push"), the spelling of Brian Keogh (Otter also "Keough" and "Keo"), and the room are unconfirmed.
items.added_by: Claude (from Nathan's Otter recordings, 9 Nov 2026)

summary.Summary:
Miguel, business developer, and Brian Keogh, chief scientific officer, presented Nuritas, a Dublin R&D company that uses its own AI platform to find bioactive peptides. The AI starts from a mechanism of action or a consumer need and returns candidate peptides for lab and animal testing, in about two years on average.

Keogh then made the case for PeptiStrong, a fava bean protein hydrolysate. The speaker says its peptides switch on muscle building through mTOR and calm inflammation through NF kappa B. In mice it prevented half the muscle lost when the hind legs were unloaded. Three human trials followed. After immobilisation, strength came back to baseline against a milk protein control. After a damaging exercise bout, strength rose above baseline within two and a half weeks. In untrained men and women, strength rose faster, with more bone mineral content as an unexpected finding.

His conclusion was that PeptiStrong boosts protein rather than competing with it, and may add to creatine, leucine and HMB.

Miguel closed on the commercial side: on-pack claims rest on EFSA protein claims, a non-hormonal sleep peptide is next, Vivatis is the partner in Central and Eastern Europe, and Nuritas is developing a product with Tantus.
summary.Key takeaways:
- PeptiStrong is a fava bean protein hydrolysate; the speaker says its peptides target mTOR (muscle building) and NF kappa B (inflammation) [03:56].
- Immobilisation trial (Netherlands, males only): the control was milk protein concentrate, not a placebo; muscle lost and regained was the same, but strength came all the way back to baseline and FSR was higher with PeptiStrong [03:56].
- KGK trial (Canada, untrained men and women): stronger quicker at day 28, kept at day 56; GDF15 fell with training load; bone mineral content rose, "a kind of a serendipitous finding" [03:56].
- Nuritas positions PeptiStrong as a booster of protein and a partner for creatine, leucine and HMB: "we're not competing with protein" [03:56].
- On-pack claims rest on EFSA protein claims; the regulatory manager has been "creatively defining" others [13:50].
- Commercial map: Vivatis formulates for Central and Eastern Europe, Nuritas has been active in Poland for six months, and it is developing a product with Tantus [13:50].

items.title: Kaneka: Ubiquinol, the active form of coenzyme Q10
items.to_check: Billed title, Oliver's surname and role, what "MTIC certified" in the UK refers to (Otter's hearing), and the room are unconfirmed.
items.added_by: Claude (from Nathan's Otter recordings, 9 Nov 2026)

summary.Summary:
Oliver of Kaneka presented ubiquinol, the reduced and active form of coenzyme Q10, which Kaneka makes in Japan. His question was why a brand should use ubiquinol rather than ordinary Q10.

His argument began with conversion. From about 30, he said, the enzyme diaphorase falls away, so the body turns less Q10 into ubiquinol; giving the active form directly gets round that. He cited a blood test in which 90 mg of ubiquinol gave the same blood level as 300 mg of Q10, and said the body cannot convert Q10 doses above 300 mg. He then listed the benefits Kaneka claims, from heart and energy to fertility, cognition and menopause, which he said rest on more than 100 studies.

He closed on Kaneka as a supplier: 100 mg a day for most people and up to 300 mg for statin users, fertility and stress; grades for softgels, gummies and other formats; halal certification; and a Belgian warehouse for short lead times in Europe.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Ubiquinol is the active form of CoQ10; the speaker says the converting enzyme diaphorase is no longer available as you get older, from about 30 [00:00].
- 300 mg of Q10 gives the same blood ubiquinol as 90 mg of ubiquinol; at 300, 600 or 900 mg of Q10 the body cannot convert more than 300 mg [00:00].
- Kaneka's dose: 100 mg a day for a normal person; up to 300 mg for statin users, energy, fertility and stress [00:00].
- Formats: pure ubiquinol for softgels, gel pills and gummies; a microencapsulated form for other dosage formats [00:00].
- Kaneka is pushing ubiquinol into active nutrition: "energy and sports" among its study areas, and a partnership with Borussia Dortmund's women's football team [00:00].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Ubiquinol is outside our range and this was a product pitch, so relevance is low.
- Kaneka lists "energy and sports" among its study areas and sponsors a women's football team, so ubiquinol is being pushed into active nutrition as a mitochondrial energy ingredient [00:00]. My reading: it will appear beside creatine in healthy-ageing active products, not against it.
- Pure for softgels and gummies, microencapsulated for the rest [00:00]. My reading: a reminder that our customers' CDMOs want an ingredient grade matched to the dosage form.

items.title: Aquanova NovaSol micellar delivery, then Balchem OptiMSM
items.to_check: Billed titles, the Aquanova speaker's name (Otter heard "Toshton Sack", the host also "Austin"), the spelling Lena Leder or Leda, the room, and the end of the OptiMSM talk (the recording stops at 12:53, a few minutes in) are unconfirmed.
items.added_by: Claude (from Nathan's Otter recordings, 9 Nov 2026)

summary.Summary:
Two short talks in one recording.

Aquanova's speaker asked how delivery technology can turn a hard-to-use, fat-soluble ingredient into a market-ready, differentiated product. His answer was NovaSol, a micellar technology. The native ingredient sits in a tiny micelle with a fat-loving core and a water-loving surface, so it dissolves in water and passes stomach acid. Processing is physical, with no chemical change, and each formulation is unique to its ingredient. The result is a liquid concentrate ready for capsules, shots and combinations. His examples were Favea's cap-in-cap product, Nourreflex PD, and the US longevity brand GVR, which built three products on the same micellar resveratrol. His conclusion: NovaSol is a bridge between delivery science and differentiated finished products.

Lena Leder, senior manager nutrition science at Balchem, then began on OptiMSM. She set it in Balchem's 33 active research projects, then described MSM as a source of sulfur and methyl groups which, she said, has shown effects on joint and skin health and exercise recovery. The recording ends about three minutes into her talk, before the data.
summary.Key takeaways:
- NovaSol is a micellar technology: lipophilic core, hydrophilic surface, water-soluble, protected from stomach acid, with no chemical change to the active [00:18].
- Each NovaSol formulation is unique to its ingredient; it is a liquid concentrate for capsules, shots and combined capsules [00:18].
- GVR, a US direct-to-consumer longevity brand, built Mind, Q Power and Glow on the same micellar resveratrol with different NovaSol actives, in vegetarian softgels [00:18].
- MSM is 34% sulfur by weight, a source of sulfur and methyl groups; supplementation "has shown" effects on joint and skin health and exercise recovery, the speaker said [10:40].
- Balchem has 33 active research projects; methylfolate is a new ingredient it hopes to bring to Europe soon [09:04].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Neither technology touches our ingredients directly, but both show what our customers' manufacturers are buying.
- Micellar delivery is a format play: it lets a capsule or shot maker differentiate on bioavailability rather than on the ingredient, and the cap-in-cap and three-product GVR examples are the finished-product systems Nick Morgan described [00:18]. My reading: delivery technology is where a CDMO earns its margin, so when we pitch creatine or clear pea protein to a Polish contract manufacturer, "which format can you make it work in" will come before price.
- Balchem supplies the same sports and active nutrition brands we serve, and OptiMSM is positioned on exercise recovery [10:40]. Relevance medium for that and for the format lesson.

- "A Novasol formulation is a water-free, homogeneous liquid active ingredient concentrate." Speaker 2 [00:18]
- "During our processing, we not chemically modify the ingredient; it's just carefully controlled physical processing parameters, which help to create the micelles around the ingredient" Speaker 2 [00:18]
- "...we have 33 active projects, ongoing research projects in Balkam, and that is over all over the whole portfolio." Speaker 3 [09:04]
- "MSM provides multiple advantages, so it is a source of sulfur, a source of methyl groups, and supplementation has shown that it has an effect on joint and skin health, and that it's supporting exercise recovery." Speaker 3 [10:40]

items.title: Martin Bauer: Rhosera, cultivated Rhodiola rosea against anabolic resistance
items.to_check: Billed title, Ralph's surname and role, the exact name of the new unit (he said "Martin Bauer Nutritions"; Otter heard "Nathan Bawa Nutraceuticals"), the room, and the spellings of the marker compounds and the Polish sites are unconfirmed.
items.added_by: Claude (from Nathan's Otter recordings, 9 Nov 2026)

summary.Summary:
Ralph of Martin Bauer Nutraceuticals, a new unit of the family-owned Nature Network, introduced Rhosera, an extract of cultivated Rhodiola rosea aimed at the ageing muscle. His question was what goes "beyond protein" for older people.

His case started with anabolic resistance. With age the muscle cell uses protein less efficiently, which is why protein advice rises from 0.8 to 1.2 g, and he said hardly any ingredient addresses that gap. Rhodiola is a well-known adaptogen, but wild supply is overharvested and adulterated, so Martin Bauer has spent 25 years cultivating its own elite lines. The cultivated root carries far more of the precursor compounds than wild material and, in muscle cells, switches on muscle-building and polyamine pathways that wild material does not unless concentrated.

The human trial put 140 untrained adults aged 55 to 75 on training and protein, with Rhosera or placebo on top. By his account soreness after exercise fell by about half on Rhosera, and strength, balance, fatigue and quality of life all improved. He called them the best results he had seen with a botanical in 31 years.

He closed with formulation advice, a dose of 250 to 350 mg, and a regulatory note: rhodiola has no EFSA claim, so brands borrow fatigue claims from magnesium or B vitamins.
summary.Key takeaways:
- The gap he names is anabolic resistance: ageing muscle uses protein less well, hence the move from 0.8 to 1.2 g of protein, and "hardly any ingredient" addresses it [00:00].
- Wild Rhodiola rosea is overharvested, adulterated with other species and, he said, listed as endangered in 2023: a supply risk for any brand built on it [00:00].
- Trial: double-blind, placebo-controlled, 140 untrained adults aged 55 to 75; both arms trained and were given protein; 400 mg of Rhosera once a day in the morning [00:00].
- Delayed-onset muscle soreness fell 46% in men and 52% in women, against 18% and 11% on placebo; the human publication is "in progress" [00:00].
- No EFSA claim on rhodiola; brands "borrow" magnesium or vitamin B claims on fatigue [00:00].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- This is the most direct talk for us. Rhosera is pitched "beyond protein": it claims to help an ageing muscle use the protein it already gets, and the trial gave protein to both arms [00:00]. My reading: a stacking partner for IsoClr: Pea and CreaWin in healthy-ageing and active-nutrition products, not a substitute, and the "protein plus an enabler" framing is one our customers will hear again.
- The soreness figures (46% and 52% against 18% and 11%) are the speaker's, from a trial not yet published; carry them with that caveat [00:00].
- His point that a brand needs a secure, cultivated supply and a clean regulatory story is one we can make for creatine too (my reading).
- The group's Polish sites and "science to shelf" service show a botanicals supplier selling directly to the same CDMOs we want to reach [00:00].
- Relevance high: muscle, protein utilisation and active nutrition for the over-55s.
summary.Quotes:
- "...there is hardly any ingredient on the market which is really trying to fill this gap by enabling a muscle cell to utilize protein more efficiently, and that was our motivation." Speaker 1 [00:00]
- "I'm in this business now 31 years, and it was the best results I've ever seen with a botanical." Speaker 1 [00:00]
- "...the delayed onset of muscle soreness. I mean, that was reduced by 46% in men, 52% in women compared to 18 and 11 percent in in the placebo group" Speaker 1 [00:00]
- "You don't have EFSA claims. You have only on old claims, or you can borrow claims like magnesia, or for magnesium, or for instance, vitamin B, to claim loss on fatigue." Speaker 1 [00:00]
summary.Follow-ups:
- Ralph's surname and role, and the exact name of the new unit (Otter: "Nathan Bawa Nutraceuticals").
- The Antioxidants paper on the preclinical work; ask for the human trial manuscript when published.
- The marker compounds he named (Otter: "rhodiolene, glycosyl, rhodiocyanide A").
- Martin Bauer's Polish sites and who they supply.
- Whether Rhosera has been combined with creatine or a pea protein in a finished product.
summary.Detail:
- The Nature Network: privately owned, fourth generation; Martin Bauer (1930, cultivation and sourcing, big in tea and RTD drinks), Finzelberg (1875, extracts for pharma and supplements) and PhytoLab (third-party lab, reference substances, contaminants); 4,300 people and over 30 manufacturing sites, several in Poland (Martin Bauer Polska and other units, as Otter heard them) [00:00].
- By 2050 probably over 2 billion people will be 60 or older; muscle loss starts unnoticed at 25 or 30 and becomes a real problem by 60 [00:00].
- Cultivation: over 25 years of experience; over 240 accessions reduced over ten years to three elite lines; seedlings raised and transplanted; controlled integrated cultivation in Central Europe with no pesticides and manual weeding, to keep out pyrrolizidine alkaloid weeds; three to four years to harvest [00:00].
- Cultivated material has the same compounds as wild, but four to five times the precursors; the clinical tests to date used wild material [00:00].
- In muscle cells the cultivated extract upregulates Pax7 (waking dormant stem cells) and MyoD (telling them how to differentiate), plus folic acid and polyamine pathways, so spermidine, spermine and putrescine are made in the cell; wild material does the same only at 2.5-fold concentration [00:00].
- Trial population: slight muscle loss but no sarcopenia, considered healthy [00:00].
- Chair stand, single-leg balance with eyes closed, bench press and leg press improved "statistically highly significant"; hand grip, which he called one of the most important biomarkers for longevity, was tested; fatigue fell significantly; quality of life, motivation and social engagement rose [00:00].
- Preclinical results are published in Antioxidants [00:00].
- Formulation: 250 to 350 mg; tablets, capsules, bars and V caps work; beverages are hard because rhodiola is very bitter; 100% plant-based, European grown, with "100% cytosy compliance" as transcribed (probably CITES; to check) [00:00].
- The group offers a service "from science to shelf" [00:00].

detail.text: The Nature Network: privately owned, fourth generation; Martin Bauer (1930, cultivation and sourcing, big in tea and RTD drinks), Finzelberg (1875, extracts for pharma and supplements) and PhytoLab (third-party lab, reference substances, contaminants); 4,300 people and over 30 manufacturing sites, several in Poland (Martin Bauer Polska and other units, as Otter heard them) [00:00].
By 2050 probably over 2 billion people will be 60 or older; muscle loss starts unnoticed at 25 or 30 and becomes a real problem by 60 [00:00].

Cultivation: over 25 years of experience; over 240 accessions reduced over ten years to three elite lines; seedlings raised and transplanted; controlled integrated cultivation in Central Europe with no pesticides and manual weeding, to keep out pyrrolizidine alkaloid weeds; three to four years to harvest [00:00].
Cultivated material has the same compounds as wild, but four to five times the precursors; the clinical tests to date used wild material [00:00].

Trial population: slight muscle loss but no sarcopenia, considered healthy [00:00].

Chair stand, single-leg balance with eyes closed, bench press and leg press improved "statistically highly significant"; hand grip, which he called one of the most important biomarkers for longevity, was tested; fatigue fell significantly; quality of life, motivation and social engagement rose [00:00].
Preclinical results are published in Antioxidants [00:00].

Formulation: 250 to 350 mg; tablets, capsules, bars and V caps work; beverages are hard because rhodiola is very bitter; 100% plant-based, European grown, with "100% cytosy compliance" as transcribed (probably CITES; to check) [00:00].
The group offers a service "from science to shelf" [00:00].

summary.Summary:
Thomas, presenting for Solabia Nutrition, opened with the brief every brand writes and every CDMO receives: clinically proven, clean label, cost-effective, innovative, ready in Q3, two-year shelf life. He called it impossible and replaced it with three questions: will they remember it, can you make it, can you prove it.

On memory, the name decides. A flavonol with a prebiotic effect went nowhere as a "flavorbiotic" and was rebranded, while an aronia berry extract renamed Brainberry is now Solabia's second biggest and fastest growing product.

On making it, briefs now ask for several grams of creatine and collagen plus botanicals in one soluble format. Creatine adds its own problem: brands want it in gummies, but heat turns it into creatinine. Solabia and the Polish CDMO Tantus avoided this with a cold-pressed tablet of creatine and a citrus extract.

On proof, he said "science-backed" means nothing on its own. What counts is the dose, the population, the endpoints and the change against placebo. Solabia has run randomised placebo-controlled trials on all its ingredients and put each study on its website. He closed by inviting brands to bring their briefs to Solabia.

- The standard brief is "impossible"; judge a launch on whether they will remember it, whether you can make it and whether you can prove it [00:01].
- Naming decides memory: the aronia extract renamed Brainberry is now Solabia's second biggest and fastest growing product [00:01].
- Briefs now ask for three to five grams of creatine and five to ten grams of collagen plus a botanical extract and a vitamin complex in one format that is soluble and mixes well [00:01].
- Creatine in gummies: heat applied over time gives creatinine, which "doesn't really do much"; Tantus's answer was a cold-pressed tablet, no heat, of creatine plus a citrus extract [00:01].
- "Science-backed" is one of the most used and most dangerous phrases in the industry; look at dose, population, endpoints and the change against placebo [00:01].

summary.Summary:
Victoria and Mateus of Tantus, a Polish CDMO, asked how a longevity trend becomes a product people actually take. Their starting point was that a trend changes nothing on its own; it matters only once a product reaches the market and becomes part of a daily routine.

Consumers want to live better, not only longer, so healthspan drives the conversation. The industry answers with new ingredients and ever more complex formulas, but they argued the right question is what makes sense in a formula, not what else can be added. Longevity is "a marathon", so format, dose and ease of use matter as much as the ingredient: a formula people will not take every day fails.

Their process runs in four steps: trend, ingredient, formula, market. Suppliers are partners who bring science and formulation knowledge, not vendors filling separate orders.

The one concept captured before the recording ended was creatine seen through a longevity lens: a chewable tablet developed with Solabia, combining three grams of creatine with a hesperidin-based ingredient and aimed at keeping physical function with age. Their line: "Chew it, don't shake it."

- Simplicity first: format, dosage and ease of use matter because consistent use is the point [02:09].
- Tantus wants long-term supplier relationships rather than transactional orders, for access to research, technical information, formulation expertise and new ideas [03:09].
- Concept one: creatine reframed for longevity, a chewable tablet with Solabia, three grams of creatine with "400 grams" of a hesperidin-based ingredient (Otter's summary gives 400 mg), tried at Solabia's stand [04:45].

items.title: The Protein Brewery: Fermotein, a fermented mycelium protein for active and all-in-one nutrition
items.to_check: Billed title and room unconfirmed; the CEO's name is transcribed "Tais Bos" (Otter titled the recording "Thijs") and the shareholder "Nova Holdings", both taken here as Thijs Bos and Novo Holdings; the nematode study partner is heard as "Nema Live".

summary.Summary:
Thijs Bos, CEO of The Protein Brewery and formerly a seller of dairy and fava proteins, presented Fermotein, a mycelium ingredient grown by biomass fermentation in Breda, in the Netherlands. His pitch was that one ingredient can carry protein, fibre and longevity bioactives together.

He said Fermotein is 50% complete protein and 30% prebiotic fibre, and is rich in spermidine and choline. It is the first mycelium protein with EFSA approval, which came this summer after five years. While waiting, the company built its market in the US, in "all-in-one nutrition": powders that sit between protein powder and meal replacement, with Ka'Chava as the model. Superfood powders are adding protein and fibre too. In Europe meal replacement is still the nearest category, and he asked the CDMOs in the room to embrace the all-in-one concept.

On evidence he cited prebiotic studies, a positive effect on GLP-1, and a nematode study in which Fermotein extended lifespan, with a human trial on a biological ageing clock planned with Wageningen University.

He closed on scale: 10 million servings sold in 2026, three US customers launched, and 70 million raised, with Novo Holdings the largest shareholder. The company is not yet profitable.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Fermotein is one ingredient with 50% complete protein, 30% prebiotic fibre (chitin and chitosan) and spermidine at about 1700 mg per kilo, used mainly in active nutrition [00:00].
- First mycelium protein with EFSA approval, "since the summer of this year" after five years; also approved in Singapore, with Australia and Canada pending [00:00].
- Market entry was the US "all-in-one nutrition" segment, between protein powder and meal replacement; Ka'Chava is the model, "super profitable", in Walmart and online [00:00].
- In Europe the nearest category is still meal replacement, not all-in-one nutrition; he expects it to come and asked the CDMOs present to embrace it [00:00].
- Evidence: prebiotic studies, a positive effect on GLP-1, and a C. elegans study in which Fermotein increased nematode lifespan by 22%; a human biological ageing clock trial with Wageningen University is planned for quarter one [00:00].

items.title: Holland & Barrett: how longevity science translates into consumer outcomes

speakers.name: Alex Glover
speakers.role: Leads the product formulation team (own-label products globally)

items.to_check: The title is from the host's introduction (heard as "how longevity science translates into the relevant consumer outcomes"), not a printed programme; Alex Glover's exact job title and the room are unconfirmed; the 2026 meta-analysis on NAD boosters he cited is not named.
items.added_by: Claude (from Nathan's Otter recordings, 9 Nov 2026)

summary.Summary:
Alex Glover leads Holland & Barrett's global own-label product formulation team. He asked how longevity science becomes something a customer will buy, and his answer was that consumers buy outcomes they can feel, not mechanisms.

He opened with a tortoise to argue that ageing badly is not biologically fixed, and said the category should be about living better, not longer. H&B's data on millions of customers showed the pattern: repeat purchase goes to products with one clearly communicated benefit, such as joint function or brain function. Its customer panels talk about playing with grandchildren and getting out of a chair, not sirtuins or telomeres.

He then turned on mechanism-led novelty. Of over 1000 customers surveyed, not one knew what NAD was, and the outcome data for the NAD boosters is very limited. Cheap interventions with strong evidence, such as fibre, vitamin D, calcium and protein, do better on evidence and on cost. Curcumin, H&B's second best-selling ingredient, was his example of evidence running ahead of the permitted claim.

summary.Summary:
Viktor Tsevsky and Matthew Kwembowski, co-founders of 2waves, pitched a platform for the three sides of the supplement market: brands, manufacturers and ingredient suppliers.

They started from a growing market, which Grand View Research puts at more than 60 billion dollars by 2030, and from how badly its sides find each other. Brands have no view of their category, offers come in no common format, inquiries are incomplete or do not fit, one inquiry runs across many email threads, and many get no answer at all. That costs time and lost business.

Their answer is a first module for new partnerships, quoting and negotiation. One inquiry reaches every manufacturer or supplier in the category. Offers come back in one structure to compare, the negotiation history stays in one place, inquiries are matched to who can make them, and every decline carries a reason. Matthew had begun on data security, with every company verified before joining, when the recording ended.

The conference organiser, Pawel Gruszczynski, sits on the project's board as strategic advisor.
summary.Key takeaways:
- The market is framed as three sides, brands, manufacturers and ingredient suppliers, with Grand View Research's forecast of over 12 percent growth a year to more than 60 billion dollars by 2030 [00:13].

- For suppliers and manufacturers: inquiries are matched to what you can produce, so you see opportunities that today never find you [02:46].
- Every company is verified before joining; the security module answers losing control of information once it sits in an inbox [07:42].
- Pawel Gruszczynski (Remedy, the conference organiser) is strategic advisor and board member of the project [02:46].

items.title: Closing panel: evidence, regulation, supply and AI in nutraceuticals

speakers.name: Alex Glover
speakers.role: Leads the product formulation team (own-label); retail and consumer perspective

speakers.name: Martina
speakers.role: From a contract development and manufacturing organisation (company not named)

speakers.name: Matt
speakers.role: Ingredient developer (company not named; spoke of a new brain ingredient and krill)

items.added_by: Claude (from Nathan's Otter recordings, 9 Nov 2026)

summary.Summary:
The day's closing panel brought together a retailer (Alex Glover, Holland & Barrett), a CDMO (Martina), an ingredient developer (Matt), a food lawyer (Joanna) and a pharmaceutical company (Alexandra). The moderator asked what each wants in the next two or three years, then turned to regulation, supply and AI.

They agreed that the consumer comes first. Alexandra wanted evidence-based claims and better communication, Martina a focus on what consumers actually need, and Alex a few claims done well, starting from the consumer's problem rather than piling on ingredients. Matt wanted a revolution in clinical trials: high-dose studies in people with real problems, published where consumers' chatbots will find them.

On regulation they differed in tone. Joanna wants food law to be a shield for innovators, though the claims system was written for vitamins. Matt was blunter: a three-year longer approval in Europe than in the US almost makes innovation impossible.

On supply, Matt warned of a fish oil shortage reaching shelves next summer. Alex described pre-bought stock and protecting the claim shoppers buy. Joanna said blaming the supplier is no defence.

On AI they wanted a human in the loop and peer-reviewed sources, and Matt warned that anyone who cannot use AI will not be able to work in two years.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Matt: trials in this industry study healthy people for short periods, so effects look small; he would run high-dose studies in people with real problems and publish, because consumers will find it through chatbots [02:52].
- Alex: consumers want evidence but not the EFSA wording; "throwing the kitchen sink" (90 plus ingredients, 35 claims) muddles the message; do a few things well for a defined audience [08:33].
- Joanna: EU food law and the claims regulation were written for vitamin C and D; innovators must combine what is legally possible with showing what trials found; food law should be "a shield", not "a heartbreak" [05:36].
- Matt: same safety package, three years longer approval in Europe than the US; cost today, income later, so the delay "almost makes the innovation impossible" [14:53].
- Matt: fish oil supply is collapsing for aquaculture now and reaches supplement shelves next summer; aquaculture buys the alternatives with higher willingness to pay [18:48].
- Alex: H&B holds up to nine months of pre-purchased stock on core lines; shoppers give three or four seconds at shelf, so protect the claim they buy (heart, eye) and find the alternative [19:36].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Two of five panellists take creatine daily, including H&B's formulation lead [00:30], [00:57]. My reading: creatine is now a default daily supplement for industry insiders, which supports CreaWin's move into everyday and healthy-ageing products beyond sports.
- A retailer and a CDMO both say the brief is the consumer problem and a few claims done well [08:33], [11:13]. My reading: our customer-facing materials should give one outcome per ingredient with the trial that shows it, not a list.
- The fish oil shortage [18:48] is not ours, but H&B's response, protect the benefit and find the alternative, shows how a retailer treats any supply shock. My reading: supply continuity and traceability for CreaWin and IsoClr: Pea are selling points to put in front of buyers now.
- Europe's three-year approval lag [14:53] means novel protein and creatine formats will launch in the US first (my reading).
- Chatbots rank peer-reviewed science [03:45]. My reading: publishing the CreaWin and IsoClr: Pea evidence where AI assistants can find it is now part of marketing.
- Relevance medium: regulation, supply and retail views, adjacent to our ingredients.
summary.Quotes:
- "I see so many brands throwing the kitchen sink at everything. It's 90 plus ingredients. It's got 35 claims on the front of the pack, and then your message gets muddled." Alex Glover (H&B) [08:33]

items.title: HMT: beyond probiotics, four new rules for the category

speakers.name: Marit Weinstra
speakers.organisation: HMT (branding and innovation agency for food and supplements)

ingredients: Akkermansia (heard as "Acromancia"; a US brand built on it)
items.to_check: Billed title, the speaker's name spelling (Otter: Marit Weinstra; the chair said "Marty Leibstra") and role, the agency's name (Otter: HMT; she says "H and D" and "HMDs"), and the room are unconfirmed; times are the recording's, Pacific converted to Polish time.
items.added_by: Claude (from Nathan's Otter recordings, 9 Nov 2026)

summary.Summary:
Marit Weinstra of HMT, a branding and innovation agency for food and supplements, opened the probiotic programme. Her question was how to win in a biotics market that has grown into a jungle of products, where consumers say they do not feel informed.

She traced four eras. Yakult made good bacteria a daily ritual. Danone Activia made digestion benefits tangible, which led brands to compete on CFU count. Then technology and survival became the story. Now the shift is from adding bacteria to nourishing the gut ecosystem, with the gut as the gateway to the rest of the body.

From that she drew four rules for winning today: quality and proof over "more is better", feeding the whole ecosystem, benefits consumers can measure and feel, and everyday food formats. Her examples came from the market: a US brand built on one Akkermansia strain, fibre brands selling plant diversity, brands setting expectations by week and month, and Poppi as a format consumers like.

Her conclusion: most of these claims cannot be made in Europe, so the brand has to carry them. A strong probiotic needs a "double IP", rational science plus an emotional brand.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Consumers say they do not feel informed about probiotics; the category has too many options and not enough clarity [00:24].
- Rule 1: 50, 80 or 100 billion CFU on shelf means nothing to the consumer; numbers alone no longer build trust, so be the proven expert in a niche, as a US Akkermansia brand does for metabolic health and weight management [03:59].
- Rule 2: talk about feeding what the consumer already has, fibres and plant diversity, which they can see and act on; fibre brands lead this language [03:59].
- Rule 3: early adopters measure with microbiome tests and apps; mass-market consumers keep buying only when they feel a difference, so brands now set expectations for one week and one month [03:59].
- Rule 4: consumers stick with formats they like; Poppi is her example of a product designed around the consumer rather than the ingredient [03:59].
- In Europe most of these claims cannot be made, so the brand must carry them: brand the strain and build a "double IP", rational and emotional [03:59].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Medium relevance: nothing was said about protein, creatine or sports nutrition, but the branding argument transfers to our customers' categories.
- The shift from "what is in the product" to "what does it do for me" is the same shift sports and active nutrition brands face with protein and creatine, and it favours ingredients whose effect a consumer notices. My reading: that is how a CreaWin or IsoClr: Pea pitch to a brand should be framed.
- "Science opens the doors, but it's a brand that keeps you in the room" [03:59]. My reading: an argument for branded ingredients with a story a European brand can tell within claim rules.
- HMT is an agency, not a buyer; it could be a partner for a customer's launch.

items.title: Novonesis and Montefarmaco: the Lactoflorene partnership, from science to consumer product

speakers.name: Ariel Annoni
speakers.role: Responsible for the Human Health business across Central and Eastern Europe, Middle East and Africa (as she said it)

summary.Summary:
Ariel Annoni runs Novonesis's human health business across Central and Eastern Europe, the Middle East and Africa. Her argument was that a successful probiotic product needs the right science, quality, manufacturing partner and brand strategy, not just a good ingredient.

She introduced Novonesis, formed from Novozymes and Chr. Hansen, with a broad portfolio and some of the most documented strains in the world. Science is strain specific, she said, and documented strains protect the reputation of the brand a manufacturer makes. The European probiotic market is growing beyond the gut, consumers read labels and expect evidence, and probiotics are no longer a niche.

Alessia of Montefarmaco, an Italian family pharmaceutical company, then told the Lactoflorene story as the proof. The partnership began in the early 2000s with an Italian requirement for a high count in a small capsule. Novonesis supplied the potency and stability, the core formula has barely changed in almost 20 years, and Montefarmaco ran a clinical study on the finished product. Lactoflorene is now third in Italy.

Their shared conclusion: a probiotic brand is built through a long-term partnership, not one ingredient. The chair closed by saying both morning talks came back to the consumer asking "what's in it for me".
summary.Key takeaways:
- Novonesis pitches to CMOs and CDMOs directly: probiotic solutions "already supported by research, market experience, and technical know-how", with the aim of a product the consumer will trust and repurchase, not only an ingredient sale [00:42].
- Science is strain specific; some strains have limited documentation, others decades of study, and documented strains protect the reputation of the brand the manufacturer makes [00:42].
- Four probiotic trends: more specialised needs, professional-recommended probiotics, applications beyond gut health, digital channels and emerging markets; "probiotic are no longer a niche category" [00:42].
- Lactoflorene: partnership since the early 2000s, started by an Italian requirement of at least 1 billion CFU in a limited-volume cap; Novonesis gave the potency and stability; core formula unchanged for almost 20 years; a clinical study on the finished product beyond what Italy demanded [09:06].
- Lactoflorene is third in Italy with around a 7% share; the three reasons given were clinical evidence, delivery innovation (the MCAP system for liquid shots) and formats for different ages and occasions [09:06].
- The partnership's value beyond ingredients: formulation expertise, consumer and marketing support, access to a pipeline of new bio-solutions [13:10].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Medium relevance: a probiotic case, but the partnership model is the one our branded ingredients compete against for a formulator's attention.
- My reading: a supplier that brings formulation help, consumer insight and a finished-product study, and keeps a formula stable for 20 years, is what a brand means by a partner; a CreaWin or IsoClr: Pea pitch to a brand or CDMO should offer the same (application work, stability, a finished-product story).
- My reading: Novonesis selling to CDMOs as a route to brands is the channel this conference exists for, and Polish CDMOs are a route for our sports ingredients too.
- Lactoflorene sells through Italian pharmacies, not our channel. No protein, creatine or sports nutrition was mentioned.
